redistricting.t: Alabama is using the 2023 Legislature-drawn map (one majority-Black district, AL-07), not the court-ordered map used in 2024. After the Supreme Court decided Louisiana v. Callais in April 2026, which narrowed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, the Court lifted the Milligan injunctions on May 11. A district court blocked the map again on May 26, and on June 2 the Supreme Court stayed that order 6–3. The Legislature nullified the May 19 primaries in AL-01, 02, 06 and 07 and held winner-take-all special primaries there on Aug 11, 2026; AL-03, 04 and 05 kept the May 19 primary and June 16 runoff.

Alaska elects one at-large U.S. House member. Under the system voters adopted in 2020 (first used in 2022), all candidates run on one open primary ballot regardless of party, and the top four advance to a ranked-choice general election. The 2026 primary was Aug 18; the general is Nov 3. Results were certified and the withdrawal deadline passed at 5 p.m. on Aug 31, when about 20 candidates withdrew, letting lower finishers move up. Senate: fourth-place Democrat David Leslie withdrew, so fifth-place Republican Gerald Heikes advanced. Third-place Dan J. Sullivan (no relation to the senator) declined to withdraw; the Division of Elections had disqualified him in June, but the courts restored him. House: Democrats Matt Schultz, John B. Williams and Yaquelin Reynoso and Republican Clay Strickland withdrew, which moved Democrat Eric Hafner and eighth-place Libertarian Jim McDermott onto the ballot. Governor: second-place Democrat Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and sixth-place Click Bishop withdrew. Fifth-place Treg Taylor was next in line, but on Aug 31 Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom declined to certify him after the Alaska Public Offices Commission voted 4–1 that his candidate financial disclosure (missing tenant names) was not filed on time. His running mate, Candice English, took the slot with Jodi Taylor as her running mate. Late on Sept 4, Dahlstrom reversed herself, citing an informal Department of Law review, and certified Taylor. General-election ballots began mailing Sept 18.

Arizona has nine U.S. House districts, drawn by the voter-created Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission (two Democrats, two Republicans, an independent chair). Its post-2020 map, first used in 2022, is unchanged for 2026. Axios (Aug 2025) reported that the commission cannot redraw mid-decade without a court order, that no challenge was pending, and that the divided Legislature/governor could not put a new map in place for 2026. No 2026 Senate race. Governor and lieutenant governor run as a joint ticket for the first time under Proposition 131 (2022), and the new lieutenant governor office takes effect in January 2027. The partisan primary was July 21, 2026, and the official statewide canvass was Aug 6, 2026. All 15 county post-primary hand counts were within the acceptable margin. No automatic recount was reported for any governor or U.S. House primary, and no source checked mentions one. In the No Labels governor primary, Lytle conceded on July 22 after trailing Hourihan by about 1,200 votes. Early ballots mailed Oct 7. The general is Nov 3, with the statewide canvass Nov 23.

al-sen-barry-moore.name: Barry Moore

oneliner.t: Three-term Republican U.S. representative from Enterprise (AL-2 2021–2025, AL-1 since 2025), former state legislator and waste-hauling business owner, who won the June 16, 2026 GOP runoff with Trump's endorsement and faces Democrat Everett Wess for Alabama's open Senate seat.

born.t: September 26, 1966, Coffee County, Alabama (birth date from Wikipedia; age 59 in May 2026 per Alabama Reflector is consistent)

upbringing.t: Moore (legal name Felix Barry Moore) grew up on a family farm in Coffee County in Alabama's Wiregrass region. He joined the Alabama Army National Guard (records reported by the Alabama Reflector date Guard service 1988–1991, followed by Individual Ready Reserve status to 1997). He earned an associate degree at Enterprise State Community College and a B.S. in agricultural science from Auburn University in 1992, where he met his wife, Heather. After a first job in the animal-pharmaceutical industry, he returned to Enterprise and started an industrial waste-hauling company with his wife. The couple have four children and attend Hillcrest Baptist Church in Enterprise.

career.role: Alabama Army National Guard (about 2.5 years), then Army Reserve (about 5.5 years); honorably discharged; basic-training active duty Mar–May 1989; never deployed
career.org: Alabama Army National Guard / U.S. Army Reserve

career.role: Co-founder/owner, industrial waste hauling and general contracting company
career.org: Hopper-Moore Inc. (also described as Barry Moore Industries / BMI)

career.role: State Representative, District 91; chaired Military and Veterans Affairs Committee

platform.t: Pledges to stand with President Trump, 'have his back and defend the MAGA agenda in the Senate'; endorsed by Trump (Jan. 2026) and VP Vance.
Secure the border, deport people in the U.S. illegally, make English the official language, prosecute officials who obstruct federal immigration enforcement.
Cut taxes (including on tips, overtime and Social Security), cut regulation and the size of government; says he will lower inflation by reducing the national debt.
Campaigned on ending stock trading by members of Congress.
Full funding for law enforcement; prosecute violent criminals and antifa-linked groups, which his site blames for the 2020 riots.
Opposes federal gun confiscation; touts an NRA 'A' rating.
Restrict women's sports to biological women and cut federal funds to those who don't; anti-abortion; opposes 'the Democrat trans agenda'.

Sponsored House bills targeting Sharia law: a March 2026 bill to bar Sharia-based discrimination by public accommodations and a May 2026 'CRUSADE Act' requiring EB-4 religious-worker visa applicants to disavow Sharia law.
Has voted for the crypto industry's top legislative priorities, holds an 'A' from Stand With Crypto, and is backed by crypto-funded super PACs.
Fund the VA, protect the GI Bill, support military families.

promises.t: Back President Trump's agenda in the Senate.
Secure the border and deport people in the country illegally.
End stock trading by members of Congress.
Lower inflation by reducing the national debt.
Cut taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.
Make English the official language.

claims.claim: Born and raised in Coffee County; grew up on a farm there.

record.t: Born in Coffee County on Sept. 26, 1966; spent much of his youth on the family farm.

claims.claim: Was the first elected official in Alabama (2016) — and, elsewhere on the same page, the first in the nation (August 2015, Mobile rally) — to endorse Donald Trump.

record.t: No independent tally of the first elected official to endorse Trump was found. The page itself gives two versions (first in Alabama in 2016; first in the nation in Aug. 2015).

claims.claim: Owns a waste removal and demolition company.

record.t: He co-founded and co-owns the industrial waste-hauling firm now called Hopper-Moore Inc. with his wife; his 2025 House disclosure lists the stake (95%) in his spouse's name.

claims.claim: Rated the most conservative member in Alabama by CPAC while in Congress.

record.t: CPAC's 2022 ratings gave Moore 91%, tied with Sen. Tuberville for highest in Alabama's delegation (one year's rating).

claims.claim: Rated Alabama's most effective legislator by the 'Center for Legislative Excellence'.

record.t: No organization by that name or rating was found. The Center for Effective Lawmaking's published Alabama scores cover 2019–2022, after he left the legislature, and do not mention him.

claims.claim: At Auburn he enlisted in the Alabama National Guard, joined Auburn's ROTC program and earned a degree in agricultural science.

record.t: B.S. agricultural science, Auburn, 1992; enlisted in the Guard while at Auburn; was on Auburn's ROTC Army Ranger Challenge Team.

claims.claim: Met his wife Heather at Auburn; married 33 years.

record.t: Met Heather Hopper at Auburn; married in 1992.

claims.claim: After college he and Heather founded BMI, Inc. with one garbage truck; it has grown for 20+ years.

record.t: Founded the waste-hauling company Barry Moore Industries in 1998 (Wikipedia), now Hopper-Moore Inc., operating 'more than two decades' (Encyclopedia of Alabama). The one-truck detail was not independently documented.

claims.claim: In 2010 he defeated a six-term Democratic incumbent to win his Alabama House seat.

record.t: He defeated Democrat Terry Spicer in 2010 (9,754–5,383). Spicer served District 91 from 1998 to 2010 — three four-year terms, not six.

claims.claim: In the Alabama Legislature he fought for military families' in-state tuition and sponsored bills to shield service members from unfair family-court procedures and to honor military spouses' out-of-state licenses.

record.t: He chaired the Alabama House Military and Veterans Affairs Committee, but Alabama Legislature bill records for these specific bills were not retrieved.

claims.claim: Serves on the House Judiciary Committee.

record.t: Serves on the House Agriculture and Judiciary committees.

claims.claim: Has passed laws to ensure veterans receive their earned benefits.

record.t: No specific enacted law was named, and congress.gov sponsorship records could not be retrieved.

claims.claim: Has repeatedly voted to cut taxes.

record.t: One such vote is documented: Aye on final passage of H.R. 1 (July 3, 2025). A full tax-vote history was not compiled.

claims.claim: Won the Congressional Management Foundation's Workplace Environment award in 2023.

record.t: CMF gave his office a 2023 Democracy Award in the 'Life in Congress' Workplace Environment category.

claims.claim: He and Heather have four children, and he still lives in Coffee County.
claims.short: Four children; lives in Coffee County

record.t: Four children; lives in Enterprise, which spans Coffee and Dale counties.

claims.claim: The 2020 riots were the direct result of radical left antifa organizations.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — Law and Order (claim 3)

record.t: A broad causal characterization, not a single checkable fact.

claims.claim: Under Joe Biden, federal law enforcement was aimed at Trump supporters and conservatives.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — Law and Order (claim 4)

record.t: A contested characterization of prosecutorial intent, not a single checkable fact.

claims.claim: In Trump's first term, working-class wages grew faster than elite wages for the first time in fifty years.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — The Economy (claim 6)

record.t: Atlanta Fed data showed the lowest-paid quarter of workers getting larger percentage raises than the top quarter since 2015, a trend that began before his term and that CBS tied partly to state minimum-wage increases. No source was found for the 'first time in fifty years' part.

claims.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill gives working families and small business owners a real tax cut.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — The Economy (claim 7)

record.t: The law cut taxes, including new deductions for tips and overtime. But CBO's analysis of the House-passed version found household resources would generally fall for the lowest-income households (largely due to Medicaid and SNAP cuts) and rise for middle and top households.

claims.claim: Under Biden the southern border 'invasion' strained police, hospitals and schools; under Trump the borders are now secure.

said.where: campaign site Issues page (barrymooreforalabama.com/issues) — Border Security and Immigration (claim 10)

record.t: 'Invasion' and 'secure' are characterizations rather than checkable measurements.

claims.claim: 'A+ rated by the NRA.'

said.where: TV ad 'Shoot You Straight' (six-figure buy, Montgomery/Birmingham/Huntsville; most-covered Moore Senate ad)

record.t: NRA ratings were not retrieved. His own Issues page says 'A rating from NRA Action', which does not match the ad's 'A+'.

claims.claim: 'President Trump endorsed me.'

said.where: TV ad 'Shoot You Straight'; also TV ad 'D.C. Garbage' (2026-04-02)

record.t: Trump endorsed Moore for the Senate in January 2026.

claims.claim: 'I've run a business, met a payroll' and 'hauled garbage.'

said.where: TV ad 'D.C. Garbage' (2026 Senate version; second most-covered Moore Senate ad)

record.t: He founded and co-owns an industrial waste-hauling company.

said.t: Opposed the Fiscal Responsibility Act, saying it would 'saddle Americans with $4 trillion in new debt'; also opposed raising the debt ceiling in 2021. Campaigns in 2026 on reducing the national debt.

did.t: Voted Aye on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act), which raised the debt limit by $5 trillion and which CBO estimated would add trillions to deficits over a decade (figures reported range from $2.8T to $3.4T depending on the estimate). The bill also contained spending cuts he supported.

said.t: 'Any threat to Israel is a threat to the United States and our freedoms.'

did.t: Voted Yea on H.R. 8034, the $26 billion Israel Security Supplemental.

saydo.topic: Tax cuts on tips and overtime

said.t: Says he fought for tax cuts on tips and overtime.

did.t: Voted Aye on H.R. 1, which enacted those deductions.

promises_prev.promise: Support a constitutional amendment limiting House members to three terms and senators to two (signed U.S. Term Limits pledge to cosponsor and vote for it; 'I support term limits for Congress').

evidence.t: He served three House terms (2021–2027) and is now seeking a Senate seat instead of a fourth House term, which fits the pledge's three-term House limit. Whether he cosponsored the term-limits amendment in each Congress could not be verified (congress.gov was not reachable).

complicating.t: The pledge commits him to cosponsor and vote for the amendment; no term-limits amendment has passed Congress. Cosponsorship status needs a human check on congress.gov.

promises_prev.promise: Keep supporting President Trump's agenda (2020 campaign).

evidence.t: He objected to Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes in January 2021 and voted for Trump's 2025 tax-and-spending law (H.R. 1); Trump endorsed him for Senate in January 2026.

complicating.t: A broad loyalty promise rather than a specific policy; listed because it was the central theme of his 2020 campaign.

wiki.t: Felix Barry Moore (born September 26, 1966) is an American politician serving since 2025 as the U.S. representative for Alabama's 1st congressional district. The district includes Baldwin, Coffee, Covington, Dale, Escambia, Geneva, Henry, and Houston Counties, as well as most of Mobile County. The largest city in the district is Mobile. From 2010 to 2018, Moore represented the 91st district in the Alabama House of Representatives.

al-sen-everett-wess.name: Everett Wess

oneliner.t: Birmingham criminal-defense and estate attorney and former Midfield municipal judge who won the 2026 Democratic runoff for Alabama's open U.S. Senate seat and faces Republican Rep. Barry Moore on Nov. 3.

upbringing.t: The public record says little about his early life. He says he has lived in Alabama since 1979, living at various points in Huntsville, Birmingham, Selma and the Mobile area. A 2016 candidate profile lists an associate degree from Selma University in 1981, followed by a computer science/mathematics bachelor's from Alabama A&M in 1985. He says he paid for college in part with a Pell Grant. He worked about a decade in software in Huntsville, then moved to Birmingham, where he earned a law degree in 2000.

career.role: Software analyst (says work included NASA payload software and Army Patriot missile systems)
Lead defense attorney for Harvey Updyke (Toomer's Corner tree-poisoning case)

platform.t: Direct federal money to rural hospitals and emergency departments, recruit physicians and medical staff, and make prescription drugs and care more affordable; also lists veterans' health care as a priority.
Campaigned on raising the federal minimum wage; blames the Trump administration for high gas, grocery and prescription prices, which he ties to the Iran war.
Opposes the budget reconciliation law for shifting SNAP costs to states and for not extending enhanced ACA premium tax credits.
Opposes the Trump proclamation expanding foreign beef imports, backs Rep. Shomari Figures' bill to nullify it, and wants wider scrutiny of tariff policy with input from Alabama farmers.

ga-sen-jon-ossoff.name: Jon Ossoff

oneliner.t: First-term Democratic U.S. senator from Atlanta, a former congressional staffer and investigative-documentary executive, who won the January 2021 runoff over David Perdue and is seeking a second term against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

hometown.t: Atlanta (grew up in Northlake, DeKalb County, metro Atlanta)

upbringing.t: Thomas Jonathan Ossoff grew up in the Northlake area of metro Atlanta. His mother, Heather Fenton, immigrated from Sydney, Australia, worked as a management consultant and co-founded NewPower PAC, which backs women running for local office in Georgia; his father, Richard Ossoff, is an attorney who owns Strafford Publications. He converted to Judaism before his bar mitzvah and grew up among relatives who survived the Holocaust. He went to the private Paideia School, and as a high-school student he interned for Rep. John Lewis. He previously held dual Australian citizenship through his mother.

education.school: Georgetown University, Walsh School of Foreign Service

career.role: National-security staffer and legislative assistant for foreign affairs and defense
Managing director and CEO; co-funded the firm with $250,000 of an inheritance
career.org: Insight: The World Investigates (TWI), London-based investigative documentary producer (BBC and other outlets)

career.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia (sworn in Jan. 20, 2021)

platform.t: Says his campaigns refuse corporate-PAC and federal-lobbyist money, backs banning corporate PACs, and sponsored a bill to bar members of Congress (and spouses) from trading stocks.
Blames Trump's tariffs, which he says Collins backed, for higher grocery and fuel costs; said Democrats would repeal them.
Calls the 2026 Iran war a 'disaster' that raised gas and diesel prices; voted in March 2026 for a war-powers resolution limiting presidential force against Iran.
Attacks the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid cuts and the expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies; campaign site says he works to expand Medicaid and protect Social Security and Medicare.
Says Americans deserve secure borders; was one of 12 Senate Democrats who voted for the Laken Riley Act in January 2025; criticizes job-site raids.
Said in the Oct. 8 debate that Georgia's voter-ID law is good; does not support the federal SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement.
Calls the U.S.–Israel relationship 'ironclad' but says support should not be unconditional; has voted both for and against Sanders resolutions to block arms sales.
Centers his first general-election ad on his bipartisan investigation of abuse in Georgia's foster-care system and his child-sex-trafficking legislation.

promises.t: Ban stock trading by members of Congress.
Ban corporate PACs (legislation introduced, per campaign).
Repeal Trump's tariffs (stated as a Democratic goal in the Oct. 8 debate).
Work to end the war with Iran.
Protect Social Security and Medicare.

record.t: Born Feb. 16, 1987, in Atlanta; grew up in Northlake in metro Atlanta.

claims.claim: His campaigns refuse contributions from corporate PACs and federal lobbyists.

record.t: Donor-side FEC data show several corporate PAC gifts were refunded (Truist $5,000 in 2021; Dell $5,000 in 2025; Citizens Financial $2,500 in 2026), consistent with the policy. But a $1,500 Lumen Technologies PAC gift (May 27, 2026) shows no refund in the data, and the campaign took about $99,500 from trade-association PACs in 2025–26 (e.g., Mortgage Bankers, National Association of Broadcasters, American Hotel & Lodging, agricultural groups). Those are industry PACs, though not single-company PACs. Individual federal-lobbyist donations were not checked.

claims.claim: Sponsored a bill to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.

record.t: Introduced legislation in January 2022 to bar members of Congress and their spouses from trading stocks. It has not become law; a Senate cloture vote on a different stock-trading bill (H.R. 7008) failed Sept. 30, 2026.

record.t: No committee markup record or news report of this was opened during research; needs a congress.gov check.

record.t: The AJC describes a bipartisan Ossoff investigation into abuse in Georgia's foster-care system, but only in reporting on his own ad; the subcommittee report itself was not opened.

claims.claim: Exposed civil-rights abuses in the federal prison system and mistreatment of military families by private housing contractors.

record.t: Wikipedia references a bipartisan investigation he led into medical mistreatment of women in U.S. detention (Nov. 2022). The specific prison and military-housing reports were not opened.

claims.claim: Studied diplomacy at Georgetown and earned a Master of Science from the London School of Economics.

record.t: B.S., Georgetown School of Foreign Service, 2009; master's in international political economy, LSE, 2013.

record.t: Interned for Lewis in high school; Lewis recommended him for his job with Rep. Hank Johnson.

claims.claim: Lives in Atlanta with his wife, Dr. Alisha Kramer, and their daughters.

record.t: Married Alisha Kramer, an Emory OB-GYN, in 2017; two daughters (born 2021 and 2025).

claims.claim: Worked to upgrade infrastructure and expand high-speed internet statewide, including $1.3 billion.

record.t: He voted for the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The $1.3 billion figure and his role in it were not traced to a source opened during research.

claims.claim: Ad 'This Is Mike Collins': Collins 'admitted' that President Trump is in the Epstein files.

said.where: Ossoff TV/digital ad 'This Is Mike Collins'

record.t: PolitiFact rated it Mostly False. Collins did say he was sure Trump was in the files, but the ad cuts his explanation that Trump appears because he alerted the FBI and banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, not because of wrongdoing.

claims.claim: Ad 'The Vote': Collins 'voted to cover up the Epstein files' on July 15, 2025, even after it was learned girls as young as 14 were abused.

record.t: Reporting confirms the ad cites a July 15, 2025 vote and that Collins later reversed his stance on releasing the files. The House roll call itself (and whether it was a procedural vote) was not opened, and no independent fact-check was found. 'Cover up' is a characterization.

oneliner.t: Two-term Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 10th District and co-owner of the family's Jackson-based Collins Trucking, who won the June 16, 2026 GOP runoff with Trump's endorsement to challenge Sen. Jon Ossoff.

upbringing.t: Michael Allen Collins Jr. was born and raised in Jackson, Georgia, son of Mac Collins, a Republican congressman for eight terms (1993–2005) who lost a 2004 Senate bid. He graduated from Piedmont Academy in Monticello in 1985 and earned a business administration degree from Georgia State University in 1990. In the early 1990s he and his wife, Leigh Ann, started Collins Trucking in Jackson; trade press traces the family's hauling business to an earlier Collins concrete-pipe company. He later chaired the board of a large Georgia credit union and served as president of the local chamber of commerce. The couple have three children.

career.role: Co-founder/co-owner; his 2025 disclosure lists a 55% interest in Collins Family Enterprises, Inc. (operating as Collins Trucking Company) and a $28,600 salary

career.role: Candidate, GA-10 (lost GOP runoff to Jody Hice)

platform.t: Runs as an 'America First' 'MAGA workhorse'; says he votes with the President 100% of the time and wants a Republican Congress to deliver Trump's agenda. Endorsed by Trump after the May primary.
Highlights the Laken Riley Act, which he authored (detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft); accuses Ossoff of weak border policy and of wanting to defund ICE and Border Patrol.
Defends Trump's tariffs as leveling the field with China and the 2025 tax cuts; blames inflation on Biden-era policy.
Blames the ACA for rising premiums and credits the 2025 law's rural-health program; says Ossoff wants a federal takeover of health care.
Backs the SAVE Act (proof of citizenship and photo ID to vote).
Says Trump 'had every right' to act to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.
Describes himself as '100 percent pro-life, period. No exceptions'; cosponsored a January 2025 fetal-personhood bill.
Called climate change 'the climate hoax' (2025).

promises.t: Help President Trump deliver his America First agenda in the Senate.
Vote with the President 100% of the time.
Pass the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship and voter-ID requirements.
Prioritize immigration enforcement in the spirit of the Laken Riley Act.

legal.t: The Office of Congressional Conduct (formerly OCE) referred a complaint to the House Ethics Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, and the committee announced its review in November 2025. The OCC report released in January 2026 found 'substantial reason to believe' Collins used official funds to pay chief of staff Brandon Phillips for unofficial or unauthorized work (possibly campaign work on government salary), and that Phillips's girlfriend was paid more than $5,000 as an intern while allegedly doing no work. Collins's lawyer asked for dismissal, saying she did work in 2023–24. After Collins fired Phillips on May 22, 2026, the committee lost jurisdiction over Phillips but continues to review Collins. No committee finding or sanction yet; the case could lapse when his House term ends in January 2027.

ia-sen-ashley-hinson.name: Ashley Hinson

oneliner.t: Republican U.S. Representative for Iowa's 2nd District since 2021 and former KCRG-TV journalist who won the June 2, 2026 GOP primary for Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat (Joni Ernst retiring), with Trump's endorsement.

hometown.t: West Des Moines area (graduated Valley High School, West Des Moines)

upbringing.t: Born in Des Moines and a graduate of Valley High School in West Des Moines; she left Iowa for college in Los Angeles, earning a broadcast journalism degree at USC, where she interned at KABC-TV. She came back to Iowa for TV news and spent more than a decade at KCRG-TV in Cedar Rapids. Her official bio says she reported on health-care costs and flooding and is a two-time regional Emmy winner. She married Matt Arenholz, an insurance executive, in 2008, and they are raising two sons in Marion. Her parents and early family life are not described in the sources reviewed.

education.school: Valley High School, West Des Moines

career.yrs: more than a decade, ending about 2016 (exact years not documented)

platform.t: Pledged at launch to be President Trump's 'strongest ally' in the Senate and deliver the America First agenda; in the Oct. 7 debate she said she would be his ally when it benefits Iowa and push back when needed.
Tighter border security and deporting people in the country illegally; supports continuing border-wall construction (2021).

Blocking regulations she says burden farmers, expanding biofuels (E15); introduced the EATS Act (2023) to block state production standards such as California's Prop 12; criticized Trump's temporary lifting of beef-import tariffs (Aug. 2026).

Says she will protect Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security; wants a bipartisan commission on Social Security solvency and is open to gradually raising the retirement age; did not back lifting the payroll-tax cap.

Says the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act lowered costs and protects Medicaid for those most in need while removing people 'gaming the system'; voted against a three-year extension of ACA subsidies in January 2026.
Voted against Iran war-powers resolutions, including in September 2026, but on Sept. 21, 2026 called for an immediate end to the war and later for pausing diesel exports and suspending the gas tax.
Tax cuts, family tax credits, help for expectant mothers and midwife access, and child-care affordability.
Promotes a proposal to bar members of Congress from trading individual stocks.
Opposes transgender girls in girls' sports; rated pro-life; voted for the Respect for Marriage Act in 2022.
Wants a stronger military and a harder line on China (supply chains, trade penalties); sits on the House Select Committee on the CCP.

note.t: From the House Clerk index, she has filed an annual report every year, each after an extension (filed in August), and one periodic transaction report, on April 5, 2021. The PDFs could not be opened. NOTUS reports her 2025 annual disclosure lists her husband's $1M–$5M interest in High Street Insurance Partners, a private-equity-backed brokerage, and that her 2021 disclosure showed him selling an interest in a private insurance company for over $1M. Democratic groups claim her net worth rose by up to $7M, 10-fold or 15-fold since she was first elected; those figures come from partisan sources and were not checked against the disclosures. In September 2026, Defend The Vote (Brian Lemek) filed a complaint with the House Office of Congressional Conduct. It alleges special access for her husband's insurance trade group and that his government-affairs role was left off her disclosure. A complaint does not open an investigation by itself; no OCC decision was reported as of 2026-10-14. She denies wrongdoing, and her campaign says her husband is not a lobbyist and has never lobbied her. She sits on the House Ethics Committee.

ia-sen-josh-turek.name: Josh Turek

oneliner.t: Democratic Iowa state representative from Council Bluffs since 2023 and two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, who won the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary for Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat.

upbringing.t: Born in Council Bluffs with spina bifida. He has used a wheelchair since childhood, and his campaign says he had 21 surgeries by age 12. His father, John, served in the Navy during the Vietnam War and later was a vocational-school administrator; Turek links his condition to his father's Agent Orange exposure. His mother, Luellen, was a social worker and community-college instructor. He grew up with three sisters and a brother; an older sister died as a toddler before he was born. He started wheelchair basketball in seventh grade, graduated from Abraham Lincoln High School, and played college wheelchair basketball at Southwest Minnesota State.

platform.t: Supports a public option and restoring ACA subsidies; would reverse the 2025 law's Medicaid cuts and repeal the One Big Beautiful Bill Act but keep its tax cuts on tips and overtime.
End Trump's tariffs (says he would vote on day one to end them); sponsor federal right-to-repair for farm equipment; year-round E15; mandatory country-of-origin labeling.
Opposes raising the retirement age; would apply the payroll tax to all income above the $184,500 cap.
Supports federal law restoring Roe v. Wade's protections; criticizes Iowa's six-week ban.
Close loopholes for billionaires and big corporations; raise taxes on the top 1% to fund the safety net.
Pass the PRO Act; end subminimum wages for people with disabilities; higher minimum wage.
Term limits for Congress and the Supreme Court; campaign against corruption and dark money.
Strengthen the border and simplify an earned pathway to citizenship.
Said in Aug. 2025 that U.S. aid to Israel should be limited over civilian harm in Gaza; calls the 2026 Iran war 'unnecessary'; keep the National Guard out of combat unless Congress declares war.
Reverse cuts to VA staffing and health care; supports adaptive sports for disabled veterans.

me-sen-susan-collins.name: Susan Collins

oneliner.t: Five-term Republican U.S. senator from Maine (since 1997) and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, seeking a sixth term against Democrat Troy Jackson on Nov. 3, 2026.

upbringing.t: Collins is one of six children of Donald and Patricia Collins, who both served as mayor of Caribou; her father, a World War II veteran, served in the Maine House and Senate. The family runs S. W. Collins, a lumber and hardware business founded by an ancestor in 1844 and now led by her brother. Her uncle Samuel W. Collins Jr. sat on the Maine Supreme Judicial Court (1988–1994). She graduated from Caribou High School in 1971 and took part in the U.S. Senate Youth Program that year, then earned a B.A. in government from St. Lawrence University (1975), magna cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa.

education.deg: B.A. Government (magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa)

career.role: Legislative assistant to Rep./Sen. William Cohen; staff director, Senate Oversight of Government Management Subcommittee (1981–1987)
Commissioner, Professional and Financial Regulation (appointed by Gov. John McKernan)
New England regional director (appointed by President George H. W. Bush)
Founding executive director, Center for Family Business
U.S. Senator from Maine; Appropriations chair since Jan. 2025; former chair of Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (2003–2007) and Aging (2015–2021)

platform.t: Argues her seniority (which she says rose from 99th to 7th) and Appropriations chairmanship let her deliver federal money to Maine; her first general-election ad featured her advocacy for $6 million toward the Eastport Breakwater.
Disputes that she votes with Trump 96% of the time, citing a roughly 70% figure; said she is 'not exactly his favorite senator.'
Calls herself the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada and cites a tariff exemption for Canadian road salt.
Says she voted to assert Congress's war-powers authority; voted against early war-powers resolutions, then backed ending the war after the April 30, 2026 War Powers deadline.
Says ICE needs reforms but that disbanding it would undermine deportation and drug enforcement; says the ICE share of the 2026 DHS money was about half of $70 billion over four years.
Says she disagrees with the overturning of Roe v. Wade; stands by her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh.
Describes herself as a strong supporter of Israel; asked in the Oct. 6, 2026 debate whether U.S. military funding should change, said the current level is good.
Blames Maine's high electricity rates on state legislative decisions, including Jackson's votes, rather than federal policy.

promises.t: Keep using her Appropriations chairmanship and seniority to bring federal funding to Maine (stated reason for seeking a sixth term).
Keep U.S. military funding for Israel at its current level.

claims.claim: Born December 7, 1952, in Caribou, Maine.

said.where: official Senate bio (collins.senate.gov/about) — campaign site not reachable

record.t: Wikipedia gives the same date and place.

claims.claim: Her family's lumber business, founded in 1844, has been run by six generations.

record.t: S. W. Collins, a lumber and hardware chain, was founded in 1844 by an ancestor; her brother Samuel is president.

claims.claim: Both parents served as mayor of Caribou; her father, a WWII veteran, served in the Maine House and Senate.

record.t: Wikipedia: both parents served as mayor; Donald Collins served one term in the Maine House and four in the Maine Senate.

claims.claim: Graduated Phi Beta Kappa from St. Lawrence University in 1975.

record.t: B.A. in government, 1975, magna cum laude, Phi Beta Kappa.

claims.claim: Appointed Maine commissioner of professional and financial regulation (1987), SBA regional director (1992), and founding director of Husson's Center for Family Business (1994).

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same posts and years (Husson role Dec. 1994–1996), plus a 1993 stint as Massachusetts deputy state treasurer that the bio omits.

claims.claim: Has cast more than 10,000 consecutive votes — the longest perfect voting record in Senate history.

record.t: She cast her 10,000th consecutive roll-call vote in early June 2026 and has not missed a vote since 1997. Sen. William Proxmire's streak (10,252) is longer, but he had missed votes earlier in his career, so hers is the longest by a senator who never missed one.

claims.claim: In 2020 became the first Republican woman to win a fifth Senate term.

record.t: She did win a fifth term in 2020 (50.98%); no independent tally of the 'first' was checked.

claims.claim: Repeatedly ranked the most bipartisan senator by the Lugar Center and Georgetown University.

record.t: The Lugar Center index itself was not opened. Separately, Newsweek notes VoteView places her among the most centrist Republican senators in the 119th Congress.

claims.claim: She has voted nine times to end the Iran war.
claims.short: Nine votes to end Iran war

record.t: Of 14 Democratic-forced war-powers votes since February 2026, she voted against five failed resolutions, then supported ending the war after the April 30 War Powers deadline. Both her 'nine' and Jackson's 'five against' are accurate counts; PolitiFact called her count selective.

claims.claim: The 96% votes-with-Trump figure is misleading; her real figure is about 70%.

record.t: BDN found the 96% figure misleading and out of date (a CQ-Roll Call subset of bills with an explicit Trump position, 95% in the first seven months of 2025). The figure Collins cited matches a separate CQ party-unity score (just over 72% with fellow Republicans), which measures alignment with her party, not with Trump.

claims.claim: More than a third of Jackson's bills died after unanimous rejection in committee.

record.t: BDN's search found about 36% of the bills he led died that way over his career, but 19% in his final two years. Her companion claim of 100 vetoes of his bills was not assessed.

claims.claim: Maine has the fourth-highest electricity rates because of how Jackson voted in Augusta.

record.t: Jackson helped enact solar subsidies projected in 2023 to cost about $225 million a year, but BDN notes these are a small part of bills; natural gas (over 40% of generation) and regional pipeline limits are the commonly cited causes. The ranking itself was not verified.

claims.claim: A Biden-era federal audit found $42 million in improper payments and fraud in Maine Medicaid autism services, and Jackson did nothing.

record.t: The HHS inspector general flagged about $45.6 million as 'improper' or 'potentially improper,' not fraud, and found similar problems in other states (at least $56 million in Indiana).

claims.claim: The ICE share of the roughly $70 billion she approved was about half, over four years.

record.t: The June 2026 law allotted about $38 billion to ICE, $26 billion to CBP and $5 billion to DHS through 2029.

claims.claim: Reports that she received illegal campaign contributions are false; Martin Kao is in jail.

record.t: Kao, a Navatek executive, pleaded guilty in 2022 to an illegal conduit-contribution scheme that sent more than $200,000 to her 2020 campaign and a pro-Collins super PAC (including $150,000 via a shell LLC to 1820 PAC); he is serving an 87-month fraud sentence. Prosecutors called her 'Candidate A' and did not accuse her or her campaign of wrongdoing; her campaign said it divested the contributions. The money was illegal on the donors' side, which the denial glosses over.

claims.claim: She is the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada and secured a road-salt exemption.

record.t: 'Most outspoken' is a characterization; the road-salt exemption was not independently verified here.

claims.claim: Advocated securing $6 million to help replace the collapsed Eastport Breakwater.

record.t: No appropriations record for the breakwater money was opened in this pass.

said.t: Said she did not believe Brett Kavanaugh would overturn Roe v. Wade; says she disagrees with the decision that did.

did.t: Voted to confirm Kavanaugh, who joined the 2022 Dobbs majority overturning Roe; she says she does not regret the vote. She was the only Republican to vote against Amy Coney Barrett (Oct. 26, 2020).

did.t: Voted against discharging resolutions to block arms sales to Israel (S.J.Res. 111, Nov. 2024; S.J.Res. 41, July 2025).

promises_prev.promise: Serve only two Senate terms (pledge made during the 1996 campaign).

me-sen-troy-jackson.name: Troy Jackson

oneliner.t: Allagash logger and former Maine Senate president (2018–2024) who was picked as the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee at a July 25, 2026 party convention after primary winner Graham Platner withdrew; he faces Sen. Susan Collins.

upbringing.t: Jackson was born in Fort Kent and raised in Allagash, a town of a few hundred people on the Canadian border. His mother, Colleen McBreairty, a teacher, had him at 16; his father, Joe Jackson, was a logger, and the two divorced when he was in middle school. At 12 he saw his father and other northern Maine loggers strike over mechanized harvesting and wages. He began logging at 19, working long shifts, often without health insurance. In 1998 he helped lead a week-long blockade of Maine–Canada border crossings to protest the hiring of Canadian loggers over Maine workers, which ended without success and led him into politics.

platform.t: Medicare for All; a moratorium on private-equity purchases of independent medical practices.
Abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE); opposes the 2026 ICE funding.
Overturn Citizens United; says he rejects corporate PAC money in this race.
Calls Israel's war in Gaza a genocide; calls for ending U.S. military aid to Israel and opposes a 'blank check'; calls Netanyahu a war criminal.
Opposes the 2026 Iran war; says the U.S. must leave to bring down fuel and heating costs.
Supports abortion rights and codifying them in federal law ('abortion is healthcare').
Union rights; higher taxes on top earners; campaigns against billionaires and corporations.

(From his 2026 governor's race) bar out-of-state private-equity and multi-state real-estate firms from buying starter homes; a higher lodging tax on out-of-state visitors and a luxury tax on vacation homes over $1 million.
Supports aid to Ukraine.

promises.t: Never vote for U.S. taxpayer-funded military aid to Israel.
Accept no AIPAC funding.
Pass Medicare for All.
Abolish ICE.
Codify abortion rights nationwide.

record.t: The 1998 blockade is documented. AP and Wikipedia describe its target as the hiring of lower-paid Canadian loggers over Maine workers, not landowner wage cuts as such, and police escorted him away. Collins's alleged unkept promise was not found in the record.

record.t: House Dec. 2002–Dec. 2008; Senate Dec. 2008–Dec. 2014 and Dec. 2016–Dec. 2024 (20 years); Senate president Dec. 5, 2018–Dec. 4, 2024.

record.t: He sponsored a 2017 generic-access law (enacted 2018 without Gov. LePage's signature) and 2019 laws creating a prescription drug affordability board and allowing importation, signed by Gov. Mills. No price-effect data was checked.

claims.claim: Passed some of the strongest reproductive health protections in the country.

record.t: Documented: 2019 abortion-coverage law and a 2023 law allowing abortion at any stage if a doctor deems it medically necessary. 'Strongest' is a characterization. Earlier in his career he had perfect Maine Right to Life scores (2003, 2010).

record.t: No legislative record for these items was opened in this pass.

record.t: Wikipedia lists an A.A. in business from UMFK (year not given).

record.t: AP and Wikipedia agree. A 2023 complaint that he lived outside his district (based on a 2019 Augusta home purchase) was dismissed unanimously by the Maine Ethics Commission, which found insufficient evidence he lived anywhere but Allagash.

record.t: BDN: the figure is misleading and out of date — a CQ-Roll Call analysis of only those bills where Trump took an explicit position (95% for the first seven months of 2025), when leaders mostly brought up bills he backed.

claims.claim: Collins voted five times against ending the Iran war.

record.t: Of 14 war-powers votes since February 2026, she voted against five; she later voted to end the war after the April 30 deadline, so the count is accurate but incomplete.

record.t: No count of Collins's public town halls was found; her campaign says she prefers individual and small-group meetings.

record.t: The Maine Independent reported her husband owns Boeing and RTX stock; her spokesperson says Collins has owned no individual stock as a senator and an adviser manages his investments. No record shows profit from the war, and a spouse's holdings are not hers.

oneliner.t: Public-health physician-trained epidemiologist, former Detroit health director and former Wayne County health, human and veterans services director who narrowly won the Aug. 4, 2026 Democratic primary for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat and faces Republican Mike Rogers on Nov. 3.

oneliner.t: Former FBI agent, state senator and seven-term U.S. House member who chaired the House Intelligence Committee (2011–2015), lost the 2024 Senate race to Elissa Slotkin by about 19,000 votes, and is the Trump-endorsed, unopposed Republican nominee for Michigan's open Senate seat in 2026.

hometown.t: Brighton Township, Livingston County, Michigan (Howell High School, 1981)

upbringing.t: Born in Livonia to Joyce A. and John C. Rogers. He spent his early years in Redford Township before the family moved to Brighton Township in Livingston County. He graduated from Howell High School in 1981 and from Adrian College in 1985 with a degree in criminal justice and sociology. He served in the U.S. Army (1985–1989), then was an FBI special agent in Chicago (1989–1994), working organized crime and public corruption. His brother Bill Rogers later served as a state representative.

career.role: Special agent (Chicago office; organized crime, public corruption)

platform.t: Bring manufacturing jobs back, cut taxes for working families, put shop classes in every high school, and lower costs. He blames Democratic policies and state energy standards for an 'artificial increase' in energy prices.
Allow tax-free 529 withdrawals for first-time homebuyer down payments, roll back housing regulations, and add incentives for builders (plan announced Feb. 2026).

Opposes 'free health care for all' and opposed extending enhanced ACA subsidies. Proposes expanding TrumpRx for drug prices and penalizing providers and insurers that don't post itemized prices or that deny care excessively.
Local control. Communities should not bear higher energy costs, and data-center tax revenue should offset local property taxes. In Aug. 2026 he backed a one-year moratorium on new data centers.
School choice, more parental involvement, and third-grade reading assessments; 'refocus schools on education'.
Counter cyber threats from Russia, China and Iran. Supported the 2025 and 2026 strikes on Iran but says the war should end soon and that Trump should seek congressional authorization for more action.
Supports Israel as the region's only democratically elected ally.
Defends Trump's immigration strategy. At the Oct. 8 debate he said ICE's efforts in Minnesota were 'probably not appropriate'.
His Oct. 2026 ad says Canada 'is not our enemy' and calls for ending the tariff war. Earlier (Aug. 2026) he said he did not know how he would vote on Senate measures condemning Trump's tariffs.
Says he will protect Social Security.

oneliner.t: Four-term Democratic U.S. representative for New Hampshire's 1st District and co-owner of Manchester's Puritan Backroom restaurant, who won the Sept. 8, 2026 Democratic primary and faces Republican John E. Sununu for the open Senate seat Jeanne Shaheen is leaving.

born.t: June 4, 1980, Manchester, New Hampshire (Wikipedia; Voteview lists birth year 1980)

upbringing.t: Christopher Charles Pappas was born in Manchester to Dawn and Arthur Pappas. His great-grandfather, a Greek immigrant, co-founded a Manchester ice cream shop in 1917 that became the Puritan Backroom restaurant, which the family still owns. He graduated from Manchester Central High School in 1998 and from Harvard College (B.A., government) in 2002, and first volunteered in politics for Jeanne Shaheen's 1996 governor's campaign. He was elected to the New Hampshire House the year he graduated. He is Greek Orthodox and married Vann Bentley in February 2023. He is the first openly gay man to represent New Hampshire in Congress.

platform.t: 'Tax Cuts and Lower Costs Blueprint': cut energy taxes, protect LIHEAP heating aid, defend clean-energy tax credits, suspend the federal gas tax (with Sen. Mark Kelly), oppose tariffs on groceries and essentials.
Says he helped cap insulin costs and let Medicare negotiate drug prices; calls for reversing health-care cuts affecting New Hampshire.

Takes no corporate PAC money (campaign claim), lead House sponsor of the DISCLOSE Act, supports overturning Citizens United and a ban on congressional stock trading, and a bill to codify the congressional ethics office.
Supports a federal law restoring abortion rights after Dobbs.
Opposes abolishing ICE; wants oversight and reforms, enforcement focused on serious criminal offenders, and due process. Voted for the Laken Riley Act in January 2025.

Backs a two-state solution and humanitarian aid to Gaza. In April 2026 said the Iran war changed his view and he would vote to limit certain arms sales to Israel; called Netanyahu's recent actions 'indefensible and unsupportable.'
Calls the 2026 Iran war a 'war of choice', supports war-powers resolutions to limit it, and calls for efforts to end it.
Leading an effort to build New Hampshire's first full-service VA hospital (campaign testimonial).
More investment in affordable housing and lower energy costs.

born.t: September 10, 1964, Boston, Massachusetts (Wikipedia; AP gave his age as 61 in October 2025, consistent)

upbringing.t: Sununu is one of eight children of John H. Sununu, later New Hampshire governor and White House chief of staff, and Nancy Hayes Sununu; his brother Chris Sununu was a four-term governor. His father's side is of Lebanese, Greek and Hispanic ancestry, and Wikipedia describes him as the first Palestinian American to serve in Congress. He earned B.S. (1986) and M.S. (1987) degrees in mechanical engineering at MIT and a Harvard MBA (1991). Before Congress he worked in high-tech, including at a company of Dean Kamen's, and was chief financial officer of Teletrol Systems, a maker of building-control systems.

More domestic production, pipelines, transmission lines and permitting reform.

nc-sen-roy-cooper.name: Roy Cooper

oneliner.t: Democratic former two-term North Carolina governor (2017–2025) and four-term attorney general (2001–2017) from Nash County, who won the March 3, 2026 primary with 92% and faces Republican Michael Whatley for the open seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis.

born.t: June 13, 1957, Nashville, North Carolina (age 68 in March 2026 per AP, consistent)

profile.residence: Nashville, NC (hometown as listed by Fox News; current residence not documented)

upbringing.t: Cooper grew up in Nash County in eastern North Carolina, attended public schools there and worked summers on his parents' tobacco farm. His father, Roy Asberry Cooper II, was a lawyer and Democratic operative who co-chaired Gov. Jim Hunt's 1976 campaign; his mother, Beverly, was a teacher. He graduated from Northern Nash High School in 1975, then went to UNC-Chapel Hill as a Morehead Scholar (B.A. political science, 1979) and UNC law school (J.D., 1982). He joined his father's law firm in 1982 and won a state House seat in 1986. He married Kristin Bernhardt in 1992; they have three daughters, and he is an elder at White Memorial Presbyterian Church.

education.school: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

career.org: Fields, Cooper & Henderson (Nashville, NC; co-founded by his father)

platform.t: Campaign centerpiece is a 'Make Stuff Cost Less' plan: ban grocery stores from using algorithms to charge some customers more, stronger antitrust rules, and separate plans on child care, housing and energy costs.
Says trade authority belongs to Congress and has pledged to vote to roll back Trump's tariffs.

Would restore the enhanced ACA tax credits, reverse the 2025 Medicaid cuts, cap drug costs, and bar insurers from denying coverage a doctor says is needed; points to the 2023 Medicaid expansion he signed.
Wants to 'recreate FEMA' and says western North Carolina has received only a fraction of the Helene recovery money it needs.
Opposes the Iran war as waged, questions the exit strategy and says Congress should take back its constitutional war-declaring authority.

Acknowledges the southern border has been tightened, supports deporting violent criminals, and called for 'immediate reforms' to ICE operations before more funding; as governor vetoed sheriff-ICE cooperation bills in 2019, 2022 and 2024.
Supports background checks and red-flag laws and has said Congress should ban assault weapons.
Vetoed North Carolina's 12-week abortion ban in 2023 (overridden).
Said in December 2025 he would support banning stock trades by top federal officials.
Says he would work with Trump when he can and oppose him when needed, and frames the race partly as Congress acting as a check.
Opposes sending public money to private schools without accountability; vetoed a voucher expansion as governor.
Opposes new voting barriers; vetoed a 2018 voter ID bill and 2023 absentee-voting restrictions.

promises.t: Vote to roll back the tariffs.
Restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits and reverse the 2025 Medicaid cuts.
Ban grocery stores from using algorithms to charge some customers more.
Bar insurers from denying coverage a doctor says is needed.
Recreate FEMA and secure more Helene recovery money for western North Carolina.
Support a ban on stock trading by top federal officials.
Push to end the Iran war and reassert Congress's war powers.

legal.t: Republican AG opponent Dan Boyce, his father Gene Boyce and two relatives' law firm sued Cooper and his campaign committee for defamation over a 2000 TV ad saying Boyce's firm charged taxpayers $28,000 an hour in a class-action tax case. A trial court dismissed the case in 2001. The N.C. Court of Appeals reversed (153 N.C. App. 25), holding that the complaint adequately alleged defamation per se and actual malice. The case went to the Court of Appeals three times. On April 16, 2014, shortly before trial, Cooper settled: his side (with its insurers, per AP) paid $75,000 plus mediation fees, and he and aide Julia White signed an apology saying that if the ad implied anything improper, they were wrong.
legal.status: Settled April 16, 2014 ($75,000 plus mediation fees, with signed apology); no finding of liability

oneliner.t: Republican former RNC chairman (2024–2025) and N.C. GOP chairman (2019–2024), a lawyer and former energy-industry lobbyist and Senate chief of staff, who won the March 3, 2026 primary with 64.6% on Trump's endorsement and is running for office for the first time.

upbringing.t: Whatley was born in Michigan and moved to Watauga County in the North Carolina mountains during his early high-school years. His father was an accountant and his mother a librarian. As a sophomore at Watauga High School he volunteered on Jesse Helms's 1984 Senate re-election campaign, and he graduated in 1987. He earned a history degree from UNC Charlotte (1991), a master's in religion from Wake Forest (1993), and a master's in theology (1994) and law degree (1997) from Notre Dame. He lives in Gaston County with his wife, Suzanne, and their three children. NBC News reported that his Michigan roots largely drop out of his campaign biography.

oh-sen-jon-husted.name: Jon Husted

oneliner.t: Republican U.S. senator from Upper Arlington, appointed by Gov. Mike DeWine in January 2025 to fill JD Vance's seat, and former Ohio lieutenant governor, secretary of state and House speaker. He was unopposed in the May 5, 2026 primary and faces Democrat Sherrod Brown in the Nov. 3 special election for the rest of the term (through Jan. 2029).

upbringing.t: Husted was born in Royal Oak, Michigan, and placed for adoption shortly after birth. His campaign says he spent his first days in foster care. James (Jim) and Judith (Judy) Husted adopted him and raised him in Montpelier in northwest Ohio, the oldest of three children. He graduated from Montpelier High School in 1985 and earned bachelor's and master's degrees at the University of Dayton. He then worked for Montgomery County Commissioner Don Lucas and at the Dayton Area Chamber of Commerce before he was elected to the Ohio House in 2000.

career.role: Staff to Montgomery County Commissioner Don Lucas
Vice President of Business and Economic Development
Lieutenant Governor; also led InnovateOhio and the Governor's Office of Workforce Transformation

platform.t: Lists lowering costs, creating jobs and making the country more affordable as core campaign themes; credits the 2025 'Working Families Tax Cuts' law and says prices must keep coming down through spending and tax cuts.
Campaigns on securing the border and attacks Brown over sanctuary policies. In Aug. 2025 he described his approach as finding a compromise, deporting lawbreakers and finding a legal pathway.

Says data-center siting is a local decision; backed legislation (July 2026) requiring data centers to pay for their own electricity, and stood with Trump on an order requiring data-center companies to fund their own power.
Describes himself as a 'champion for life'; endorsed by National Right to Life, Ohio Right to Life and SBA Pro-Life America.
Says he defends Second Amendment rights (A rating from Buckeye Firearms Association, per his campaign) and supports law enforcement; campaign cites 75 sheriff endorsements.
Has proposed removing people in the U.S. illegally from Medicaid to save money (July 2025); argued in 2021 that Medicaid without work requirements undermines the work ethic.
Supports sanctions on Russia unless it pursues a lasting peace with Ukraine.

promises.t: Keep his focus on 'delivering for Ohio's working families' in a full term: lower costs, create jobs, secure the border.
Bring prices down through spending cuts and tax cuts.
Make data centers pay for their own power rather than passing costs to ratepayers.

record.t: Ohio Secretary of State, Jan. 2011–Jan. 2019; elected 2010 and 2014.

record.t: He served as lieutenant governor from Jan. 2019 to Jan. 2025, about six years, which is one full term plus two years of a second term that he left when appointed to the Senate. The page's wording appears to date from his first term.

record.t: No independent source comparing Ohio income-tax cuts by size was opened in this pass.

claims.claim: As Secretary of State, made Ohio 'the least costly state in the Midwest to start and maintain a business.'

record.t: The page gives no source or ranking, and none was found. Wikipedia records that he cut the office's budget by $14.5 million and about a third of its staff.

claims.claim: As Lt. Governor, founded InnovateOhio to cut costs and government waste, saving 'millions' of taxpayer dollars.

record.t: He led the newly created InnovateOhio and listed himself as its director (2019–2025) on his Senate disclosure. No audited savings figure was found.

claims.claim: Helped bring Intel's chip plant, 'the largest economic development deal in state history.'

record.t: No source documenting his personal role in the Intel deal was opened in this pass.

record.t: His disclosure lists him as director of the Governor's Office of Workforce Transformation (2019–2025), which fits the claim, but no program record was opened.

record.t: Wikipedia's election record shows him winning every general election he contested from 2000 (Ohio House) through 2022 (lieutenant governor, on DeWine's ticket). He ended his 2018 governor bid before the primary to become DeWine's running mate, so it was not a loss.

record.t: Brown was first elected to the Ohio House in 1974, but he was out of office from early 1991 to Jan. 1993 after losing the 1990 secretary-of-state race, and again since Jan. 2025. 'Creature of Washington' is opinion.

oh-sen-sherrod-brown.name: Sherrod Brown

oneliner.t: Democratic former U.S. senator (2007–2025) and congressman from Ohio, three-term Senate Banking Committee leader who lost his seat to Bernie Moreno in 2024, now the Democratic nominee in the 2026 special election against appointed Sen. Jon Husted.

upbringing.t: Brown was born and raised in Mansfield, Ohio. His mother was Emily Campbell Brown and his father, Charles Gailey Brown, was a physician. He became an Eagle Scout in 1967 and graduated from Mansfield Senior High School in 1970. He earned a B.A. in Russian studies at Yale in 1974, the same year he was elected to the Ohio House. He later earned an M.A. in education (1979) and an M.P.A. (1981) at Ohio State and taught at its Mansfield branch campus. He is married to Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist Connie Schultz.

career.role: Ohio Secretary of State (lost 1990 reelection to Bob Taft)

platform.t: Lists affordability and health-care cost reform as his core issue: take on insurers, lower prescription prices for seniors, and cap seniors' insulin costs at $35.
Restore pensions for retirees he says were 'fleeced by Wall Street' and restore Social Security benefits for Ohio workers.

Opposes large tax breaks for billionaires and corporations. He says he re-entered politics because of the 2025 tax-and-spending law, which he calls a 'rigged system' that cut programs such as Medicaid.
Runs on a pro-worker, pro-union agenda and attacks tariffs for raising prices. He opposed NAFTA and later backed USMCA as a step toward pro-worker trade.

Calls for ending Ohio's data-center tax break, limiting data centers' water use and keeping their electricity costs off consumers' bills; says Ohioans should decide whether data centers are built in their communities.
As Banking chair he called for comprehensive crypto legislation after the FTX collapse. He says crypto should expand opportunity without putting Ohioans at risk.

promises.t: Cap seniors' out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 and lower prescription-drug prices.
Restore pensions for retirees and Social Security benefits for Ohio workers.
End Ohio's data-center tax break and keep data centers' power costs off household bills.
Fight tax breaks for the wealthy and cuts to programs like Medicaid.

wiki.t: John Francis Reed (born November 12, 1949) is an American politician, lawyer, and former Army officer serving as the senior United States senator from Rhode Island, a seat he was first elected to in 1996. A member of the Democratic Party, he was the U.S. representative for Rhode Island's 2nd congressional district from 1991 to 1997. Reed graduated from the United States Military Academy and Harvard University. He served in the U.S. Army on active duty as an infantry officer in the 82nd Airborne Division from 1971 to 1979 and as a reservist from 1979 to 1991, retiring with the rank of Major. He has been the dean of Rhode Island's congressional delegation since John Chafee died in 1999.

oneliner.t: Texas attorney general since 2015 and former state legislator who unseated Sen. John Cornyn in the May 26, 2026 Republican runoff (63.8% to 36.2%) after Trump endorsed him, and now faces Democrat James Talarico for the U.S. Senate.

born.t: December 23, 1962, Minot Air Force Base, Minot, North Dakota (born Warren Kenneth Paxton Jr.)

hometown.t: Raised in a moving Air Force family, mostly in California; graduated high school in Lawton, Oklahoma

upbringing.t: Paxton's father served in the U.S. Air Force, and the family of five lived in a trailer that moved with his postings, including Florida, New York, North Carolina, California and Oklahoma. He spent much of his childhood in California and graduated from MacArthur High School in Lawton, Oklahoma. He earned a psychology degree and an MBA at Baylor University, then a law degree at the University of Virginia. He married Angela Allen in 1986, and they have four children. Angela Paxton later became a Texas state senator. (These details come from one secondary source only.)

platform.t: Ran as a senator who would support Trump on his priorities and 'stand up and fight for Republican values'; casts himself as an America First conservative. Trump endorsed him on May 19, 2026.

Cut taxes and stop wasteful spending.
Tied his decision to stay in the primary to a demand that the Senate end the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act, a voter-citizenship bill.
End shipments of abortion pills into Texas.
Stand with Trump to protect gun rights.
As attorney general, defended Texas's anti-BDS law and reaffirmed it in October 2023. In August 2025 he opened an investigation into Plano ISD over alleged antisemitism and anti-Israel curriculum.

legal.t: A Collin County grand jury indicted him in 2015 on three felony securities-fraud counts. He was accused of soliciting investors for a Texas tech startup without disclosing that he was being paid in company stock, and he pleaded not guilty. In March 2024 he entered an 18-month pretrial intervention agreement with no plea and no admission of guilt. Under it he paid $271,000 in restitution, did more than 100 hours of community service and completed ethics training (30 hours, against 15 required). The charges were dismissed on June 18, 2025, in Harris County district court.
legal.status: Dismissed June 18, 2025 after he completed pretrial intervention; never convicted

legal.t: The Texas House impeached him 121–23 on May 27, 2023, on 20 articles alleging bribery and abuse of office, centered on favors for donor Nate Paul and the firing of whistleblowers. The Senate acquitted him on all 16 articles it tried on Sept. 16, 2023. No article got more than 14 of the 21 votes needed, and only two Republican senators voted to convict on any article. The Senate dismissed the other four articles, which concerned the securities case, by a 19–11 vote. His wife, Sen. Angela Paxton, was barred from voting.
legal.status: Acquitted Sept. 16, 2023; reinstated as attorney general

legal.t: Eight top aides reported him to the FBI in 2020, alleging bribery and abuse of office to help Nate Paul. A federal grand jury examined the matter, and the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section took it over in 2023. AP reported on 2025-04-03, citing anonymous sources, that DOJ decided in the final weeks of the Biden administration not to prosecute. A senior career official reportedly recommended against charges over doubts about winning a conviction, while the West Texas prosecutors who first handled the case reportedly believed the evidence supported an indictment. DOJ has not commented publicly.
legal.short: Federal corruption probe; no charges filed
legal.status: No federal charges ever filed. DOJ's decision not to prosecute is reported by AP sources, not officially announced

legal.t: The SEC filed a civil fraud suit in April 2016 over his solicitation of investors before he took office. On March 2, 2017, U.S. District Judge Amos Mazzant dismissed it with prejudice, finding he had no plausible legal duty to disclose his compensation arrangement.
legal.status: Dismissed with prejudice March 2, 2017

legal.t: Signed an agreed order with the Texas State Securities Board for acting as an investment adviser representative for Mowery Capital Management without registering. It carried a reprimand and a $1,000 fine.
legal.status: Agreed order; reprimand and $1,000 fine (2014)

legal.t: Four former top deputies fired after reporting him to the FBI sued under the Texas Whistleblower Act in November 2020. In April 2025, Travis County District Judge Catherine Mauzy found the attorney general's office violated the act and awarded $6.6 million. Paxton dropped the office's appeal in July 2025. The judgment is against the agency, and Texas taxpayers pay it.
legal.status: Final judgment against the Office of the Attorney General after the appeal was dropped (July 2025); payment requires a legislative appropriation

legal.t: The State Bar's Commission for Lawyer Discipline sued him in May 2022, alleging he made false claims in the 2020 Texas v. Pennsylvania election suit. After the Texas Supreme Court threw out a parallel case against his deputy on separation-of-powers grounds (Dec. 2024), the bar dropped its case. The Supreme Court dismissed it as moot in January 2025.
legal.short: Bar discipline suit dropped, dismissed moot
legal.status: Dismissed as moot, January 2025, after voluntary dismissal; no ruling on the merits

born.t: May 17, 1989, Round Rock, Texas (born James Dell Collins)

upbringing.t: His mother, Tamara, left his biological father when James was seven weeks old. Wikipedia describes the father as an abusive alcoholic. A few months later she married Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname. He went to Round Rock ISD schools and graduated from McNeil High School. His maternal grandfather, Jimmy Causey, was a Baptist preacher in South Texas. He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in 2018, the year he was first elected. platform.t: His August 2026 'New American Dream' plan would repeal tax cuts for the top 1%, create universal childcare and paid family leave, help first-time homebuyers with down payments, and cap credit-card interest rates. He calls trickle-down economics a 'false gospel.'
Universal coverage through a Medicare buy-in ('Medicare for Y'all') open to every age, and breaking up vertically integrated health-care companies.
An 'all-of-the-above' energy plan (oil, gas, nuclear, wind, solar, geothermal); suspend federal gas and diesel taxes; end tax incentives for data centers and make them pay for infrastructure.

Calls himself a 'border security Democrat.' Backs the bipartisan Dignity Act and pathways for some undocumented immigrants, and would redirect ICE funding. In January 2026 he called for prosecuting ICE agents who abused their power.
Supports a two-state solution and banning offensive weapons sales to Israel. Has accused Israel of war crimes. Refuses support from AIPAC and J Street.
Refuses corporate PAC money and says he returns checks from companies such as Walmart and Chevron. Frames the race as 'top vs bottom,' not left vs right.
Supports legal abortion.
Protect the Second Amendment and establish universal background checks.
Opposes private-school vouchers and education savings accounts.
Remove the Trump administration's tariffs on farm inputs.

oneliner.t: Republican U.S. senator from Alabama since January 2021 and former college football head coach (Ole Miss, Auburn, Texas Tech, Cincinnati), Trump-endorsed nominee for governor whose eligibility under the seven-year residency rule is being challenged in court.

born.t: September 18, 1954, Camden, Arkansas (Wikipedia; Senate bio does not state birthplace — single secondary source)

upbringing.t: Tuberville grew up in Camden, Arkansas, one of three children of Olive Nell (Chambliss) and Charles R. Tuberville Jr.; his Senate biography says his father was a World War II veteran awarded five Bronze Stars and a Purple Heart. He graduated from Harmony Grove High School in 1972 and earned a physical-education degree from Southern State College (now Southern Arkansas University) in 1976. He then spent about four decades in college coaching, including assistant jobs at Miami and Texas A&M before head-coaching jobs in Mississippi, Alabama, Texas and Ohio.

platform.t: Eliminate the state grocery tax, 'cut taxes even further', and 'audit every state dollar'; pitches 'less taxes, more results'.
Protect school choice and the CHOOSE Act education savings accounts; reward good teachers and hold poor ones accountable; workforce focus.
Says he will send the National Guard into Montgomery (which he calls a 'war zone'), Birmingham and Mobile on day one.

Supports data-center growth but says they must 'pay full taxes' at the highest property-tax rate, get no tax breaks or abatements, pay for their own power, avoid fresh drinking water for cooling, and that communities get 'the final say'; opposes a moratorium.
Opposes the Affordable Care Act (under which Medicaid expansion is offered) and has supported individual health savings accounts.
Launch themes: oppose 'woke ideology', create jobs, improve education, border security.

promises.t: Eliminate Alabama's state grocery tax.
Audit every state dollar.
Send the National Guard into Montgomery, Birmingham and Mobile 'on Day One'.
End tax breaks for data centers, tax them at the maximum property-tax rate, and let communities decide where they are built.
'I will protect Alabamians from paying a single cent more for their energy' (data centers).
Protect the CHOOSE Act school-choice program.

claims.claim: "My wife and I, Suzanne, moved here over 25 years ago."

record.t: He became Auburn's head coach in 1999, so he first moved to Alabama more than 25 years before 2025. But the record shows long periods elsewhere: head coach at Texas Tech (2010–12) and Cincinnati (2013–16); in a 2017 ESPN video he said he had retired to Santa Rosa Beach, Florida; his Florida beach home got a Florida homestead exemption in 2018; he voted in Florida in November 2018 and registered to vote in Alabama on March 28, 2019.

claims.claim: "I live in Auburn." (also the residence stated on his Senate biography)

said.where: remarks reported by 1819 News; Senate 'About' page

record.t: Disputed and in litigation. The Auburn (Cherry Street) house has carried an Alabama homestead exemption since 2018, but property records showed it owned by his wife and son until he was added to the deed on May 7, 2024. A 2023 Washington Post analysis cited campaign-finance and property records pointing to the Santa Rosa Beach, Florida, home. He has said he spends 'a few days a month' in Destin, Florida. No court has ruled on the facts: a quo warranto suit was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction (July 9, 2026) and the appeal was fully briefed at the Alabama Supreme Court as of Sept. 4, 2026.

claims.claim: "Unlike Doug Jones, Coach has also accepted ZERO PAC (political action committee) money."

said.where: campaign manager Jordan Doufexis statement to Alabama Reflector

record.t: The same Alabama Reflector review of his state filings found about $10,000 in PAC contributions (Diversified Gas & Oil PAC $2,500; Travelers PAC $2,500; Home Depot PAC $5,000) plus in-kind PAC contributions (BANKPAC $3,600; Truk PAC $7,200; Alabama Farm PAC nearly $3,000). His campaign has said it returns PAC checks; the filings reviewed still show the contributions above.

claims.claim: He "helped pass the largest working-class tax cuts in history" (One Big Beautiful Bill Act).

said.where: first TV ad ('Less taxes, more results')

record.t: There is no standard measure of a 'working-class' tax cut. PolitiFact found the 2025 law is not the largest tax cut in U.S. history as a share of GDP (third since 1980 counting the extended 2017 cuts; tied for seventh counting only new cuts) and noted some lower-income families may pay more because enhanced ACA premium credits were not extended. His Yea vote on the law is covered in the separate key-votes file.

claims.claim: He "delivered Alabama's biggest tax refund ever."

record.t: No Alabama-specific refund total was found. Yellowhammer News noted only a national Treasury figure (average refund above $3,400, up 11%). Federal refunds also are not delivered by one senator.

claims.claim: Delivered "over $2,800 in annual savings" on taxes for Alabama.

said.where: first TV ad (as described by ADN)

record.t: The ad's source for $2,800 was not found. Sen. Katie Britt's 2025 op-ed on the same law used a different figure (an average $2,200 tax increase avoided) and gave no source.

claims.claim: Opponents' education plan "kicks tens of thousands of children out of the school of their choice."

record.t: More than 34,000 students were approved for CHOOSE Act accounts for 2026–27, so 'tens of thousands' matches program size. But Jones said on July 29–30, 2026: 'The kids that are in there now, let them finish, but quit taking applications.' He later vowed to 'stop the CHOOSE Act in its tracks' without saying current students would lose funding.

claims.claim: Montgomery is a "war zone"; Mobile and Birmingham are "dangerous."
