democracy.t: After the 2020 election, likened results to referees adding touchdowns after a game ended — AP described this as backing Trump's unsupported fraud claim.
As senator-elect signaled he would join an objection to the Electoral College count ('You'll see what's coming'); Trump called him a 'hero'.
One of six senators who voted to sustain the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (failed 6–93).
One of seven senators who voted to sustain the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (failed).
Voted against creating an independent commission on the Jan. 6 attack; told ABC News in 2025 he fully supported Trump's Jan. 6 pardons.
Told Steve Bannon that Democrats 'stole the election from President Trump' in 2020.
Said on Newsmax 'we probably have four or five senators that didn't legally win', offering no evidence or names.

note.t: Born and raised in Arkansas. Lived in Alabama as Auburn's coach (1999–2008); coached in Texas and Ohio 2010–2016; said in 2017 he had retired to Santa Rosa Beach, FL, and voted in Florida in Nov. 2018; registered to vote in Alabama March 28, 2019. Whether he has been an Alabama resident since Nov. 2019 (the seven-year test) is the subject of a pending Alabama Supreme Court appeal, so a year count is not given.

eligibility_challenge.t: Two veterans (Brooke Lynn Dorgan and Justin Jude LeBlanc) filed a quo warranto suit claiming he does not meet the Alabama Constitution's seven-year residency requirement for governor. Montgomery Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed it July 9, 2026 for lack of jurisdiction, without ruling on the facts. Plaintiffs appealed July 14. Tuberville, AG Steve Marshall and the Alabama GOP asked the court to affirm, and briefing closed Sept. 4, 2026. No decision was found as of Oct. 8, 2026. A separate primary challenge by Ken McFeeters was dismissed by the state GOP committee on June 14, 2026. To rebut that challenge, his lawyers filed seven years of redacted Alabama income-tax returns (June 1, 2026); the Alabama Department of Revenue declined a records request to confirm his state filing status.

checks.legal: CourtListener and efile/eFD domains were blocked by this environment's proxy, so federal dockets were not searched directly. Searched news archives (AP, APR, Alabama Reflector, ADN, Lagniappe, CNBC, Wikipedia) for civil/criminal cases, Senate Ethics matters and STOCK Act complaints. Found: the 2012–2013 TS Capital investor suit (settled), the 2021 STOCK Act late filings and CLC complaint to Senate Ethics (no public outcome found), and the 2026 residency quo warranto case (pending appeal). Alacourt is paywalled and was not searched. UPDATE 2026-10-14: the residency quo warranto appeal was decided Oct. 9, 2026 (Alabama Supreme Court affirmed dismissal for lack of jurisdiction; merits never reached). CourtListener/Justia still unreachable, so courts stays 'news'.
checks.foreign: FARA: the bulk FARA files (all registrants, short-form registrants, foreign principals) were searched by exact name on 2026-10-13 by the records collector and re-checked here; the loose name matches in that output are other people, and nothing matches this candidate. News and the 2020 Senate disclosure (secondary copy) show no foreign-government or foreign-business ties; the only foreign item found was trading in a China-based company's securities (Alibaba options, 2021).
checks.claims: Fixed sample: the campaign site coachforgovernor.com (bio and issues pages) could not be opened (proxy block). Bio claims came from his launch speech and Senate bio. Campaign claims came from his three most-covered 2026 TV ads ('Less taxes, more results', the 'Smarter Plan' school-choice ad, the National Guard crime ad) and his campaign's PAC-money statement. Ad spending is unknown; ADImpact reported about $11,000 digital for the school-choice ad. UPDATE 2026-10-08: coachforgovernor.com still blocked (direct fetch refused; web.archive.org copy blocked). As a stand-in for the campaign bio page, rated the checkable facts on his own Senate 'About Coach' page (4 bio claims). The data-center ad of Oct. 6, 2026 (1819 News) was not added because the sample already uses the most-covered ads.
checks.democracy: NPR/GPB list of Jan. 6–7, 2021 objectors; PBS/AP; Senate Democrats floor record; AP Nov. 2020; Scripps Dec. 2020; Mediaite 2024 and 2026; Wikipedia. senate.gov roll-call pages could not be fetched. Re-checked 2026-10-08: NPR list via GPB lists him among the 6 senators sustaining the Arizona objection (93–6) and the 7 supporting the Pennsylvania objection. The Senate Democrats floor page confirms the 6–93 Arizona tally but does not list names. Official senate.gov roll-call pages were still unreachable, so the item stays 'news'. UPDATE 2026-10-14: certification votes confirmed from the Senate roll-call records themselves (votes 1 and 2 of the 117th Congress, 1st session, read by the records collector: Yea on both objections). Public statements on 2020 (Nov–Dec 2020, Nov 2024 Bannon interview) and 2026 already sourced, so democracy is 'done'.

legal.t: Seven investors sued him, partner John David Stroud and their TS Capital entities in federal court in February 2012 (an eighth joined later), alleging securities fraud. Stroud pleaded guilty to criminal securities fraud and got 10 years. Tuberville was never charged (investigators said he was also a victim) and settled with the plaintiffs under sealed terms on Oct. 8, 2013.
legal.status: Settled (sealed), Oct. 8, 2013

legal.t: Reported about 130 stock and option trades from Jan.–May 2021 (worth $894,000 to $3.5 million) after the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline. His office said he was unaware of the trades, filed the report, and paid the late-filing penalty. The Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the Senate Ethics Committee on July 29, 2021.
legal.status: Late-filing penalty paid; no public Senate Ethics action found

foundation.t: Tommy Tuberville Foundation (founded 2014) raised $289,599 and spent $51,658 (about 18%) on charitable causes in 2014–2018, per APR's review of tax filings; his campaign cited unrecorded donated labor and speaking fees.

military_holds.t: Blocked about 445 senior military promotions for most of 2023 to protest a Pentagon abortion-travel policy. He dropped most holds Dec. 5, 2023, kept holds on four-star officers, and ended them Dec. 19, 2023.

oneliner.t: Democratic former U.S. senator (2018–2021) and former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama who prosecuted two Klansmen for the 1963 16th Street Baptist Church bombing, now the Democratic nominee for governor.

born.t: May 4, 1954, Fairfield, Alabama (Wikipedia; The Atlantic gives his age as 72 in July 2026, consistent)

hometown.t: Fairfield, Alabama (grew up there; Fairfield High School)

upbringing.t: Jones (legal name Gordon Douglas Jones) grew up in Fairfield, a steel town just west of Birmingham. His father, Gordon, worked at U.S. Steel and his mother, Gloria, was a homemaker; one grandfather was also a steelworker and the other a coal miner, and Jones worked in a steel mill while in school. He graduated from Fairfield High School, the University of Alabama (B.S. political science, 1976) and Samford University's Cumberland School of Law (J.D., 1979). He married Louise New in 1992; they have three children.

platform.t: One-year moratorium on data centers; no tax breaks for data-center companies; ban secret deals and nondisclosure agreements; public notice and impact studies.
Suspend the state gas tax when prices spike; fully eliminate the grocery tax; raise wages, including the minimum wage; end taxes on overtime; accountability at the Public Service Commission.
State earned income tax credit, more child care, free community college for adults without credentials, apprenticeship incentives, occupational-licensing changes.
Expand Medicaid; use the money to strengthen rural hospitals and mental-health and addiction services.
Ban elected officials from trading individual stocks; stronger state financial-disclosure rules; citizen ballot initiatives; expand early voting.
Put a state lottery before voters, with revenue going to voter-chosen priorities.
Opposes the CHOOSE Act education savings accounts: let current students finish but stop new applications.
Partner with localities on affordable housing; independent oversight and reform of the prisons, which his platform calls dangerous and unconstitutional.

Fully eliminate the state grocery tax.
Expand Medicaid.
Ban elected officials from trading individual stocks while in office.
Put a state lottery before voters.
Stop new CHOOSE Act applications and let current participants finish.
Create a state earned income tax credit and free community college for adults without credentials.

claims.claim: Expanding Medicaid would cover "more than 154,000 working Alabamians."

said.where: campaign Priorities page (item 4, as of access date)

record.t: Families USA (March 2026) estimates about 154,842 low-income adults could enroll under expansion after removing an estimated 36% who would lose coverage under new federal work-reporting rules. Alabama Arise cites 'up to 155,000.' The figure matches these advocacy estimates, but the source does not count how many are 'working'; it is the number expected to remain enrolled under work reporting.

claims.claim: Alabama is turning down "roughly $182 million in federal healthcare funding each year."

record.t: The number matches Families USA's estimate of $181.6 million for 2026, but that figure is state costs and lost savings (uncompensated care, existing Medicaid groups, mental health, inmate inpatient care) that federal expansion money could cover. It is not the total federal expansion funding forgone, which would be larger. The estimate comes from an advocacy group, drawing on PARCA's 2022 study.

claims.claim: "Data center developers are getting big tax breaks from Montgomery, and Tommy Tuberville is taking their money."

record.t: Alabama law has allowed data-center tax abatements of up to 30 years. A 2026 bill to cap them at 20 years passed the Legislature in April 2026; whether the governor signed it was not confirmed. Tuberville's state filings show a $25,000 contribution in August 2026 from Applied Digital Corp., a Dallas data-center developer tied to a proposed Brookwood project.

claims.claim: Tuberville called residents' concerns about electric bills, water use and harm to communities and the environment "bullcrap."

said.where: first TV ad (as described by ADN)

record.t: On July 13, 2026, Tuberville said of the claim that data centers will ruin the climate: 'bull crap.' In the same remarks he blamed opposition on Chinese social-media influence. The recorded remark was about the climate claim. It was not shown to be about electric bills or water, and on July 23 he said he understands why Alabamians might be hesitant.

claims.claim: Tuberville made more than 1,300 stock trades in the Senate, more than 250 involving AI or data-center companies (worth $5.2M–$14M), including 14 Alibaba trades.

record.t: The total fits Quiver Quantitative's count of 1,356 trades as of Oct. 2025. The AI/data-center subtotal and the Alibaba count could not be checked against Senate eFD (blocked). Disclosures give value ranges, so dollar totals are inherently imprecise. Jones did not allege any law was broken.

claims.claim: Tuberville is "wrong" on data centers (with his past remarks on gas prices).

record.t: Policy judgment. The gas-price remarks quoted in the ad could not be read (paywall).

claims.claim: "No one has ever — ever — questioned my being an Alabama resident for my entire life."

record.t: Records support Alabama residency: he and his wife have claimed a homestead exemption on their Mountain Brook home continuously since buying it in 2010. But after leaving the Senate he worked from ArentFox Schiff's Washington office, and more than 25 FEC receipts and a PAC record list that D.C. address. Lagniappe was questioning his records when he made the statement. He declined to share state tax receipts.

claims.claim: Data center developers are getting 'big tax breaks from Montgomery.'
claims.short: Data centers get big state tax breaks

said.where: first TV ad (30 seconds, broadcast and cable), as described by Alabama Daily News

record.t: Alabama's data-center tax abatements could run up to 30 years with no investment requirement. HB 399 (2026), which passed the Senate April 9, 2026 and went to the governor, caps them at 20 years (plus 10 more for qualifying local investment) and makes centers over 100MW pay some state taxes. Whether the governor signed it was not checked.

claims.claim: Tuberville is 'pushing to build AI data centers across Alabama.'

said.where: first TV ad (30 seconds, broadcast and cable), as described by Alabama Daily News

record.t: Tuberville is on record as a vocal supporter of data-center expansion in Alabama. But he attaches conditions: data centers must pay for their own power and infrastructure and not use fresh drinking water. His Oct. 6 ad also promises to end data-center tax breaks and let communities decide where they go. Supporting expansion is documented; the ad leaves out these conditions.

said.t: Said if Tuberville released his Alabama and federal income tax returns showing his home residence, 'I will do the same.'

did.t: Tuberville filed seven years of redacted Alabama returns on June 1, 2026 (federal returns not reported released). As of Aug. 10, 2026, Jones had not released his and did not respond to follow-up questions.

entries.t: 'The kids that are in there now, let them finish, but quit taking applications.'
Called the program 'ill-conceived' and vowed to 'stop the CHOOSE Act in its tracks', ending it or rolling back key parts before income limits lift in 2027.
Called for a six-month to one-year moratorium on permitting new data centers.
One-year moratorium on approvals of large data centers, an end to NDAs, and public input before deals.
Cited his work as senator pushing Alabama to expand Medicaid.
Campaigns on expanding Medicaid.
Proposes barring statewide officials from trading stocks and holding related investments for five years after leaving office.

votes.bill: S. 1, Strengthening America's Security in the Middle East Act of 2019
votes.what: Passed 77–23. The bill included security aid for Israel and provisions allowing state and local governments to penalize boycotts of Israel (BDS).

pac_note.t: Itemized PAC money reported by news outlets: two PACs (Speak Up PAC, Blue Hen Federal PAC) totaling $3,500 in December 2025 plus $1,000 from Sen. Duckworth's committee; 'just over $25,000' from PACs Dec. 2025–July 2026 (also IBEW PAC $5,000, United Steel Workers District 9 $5,000, Marengo County Democratic Executive Committee $3,000, GoDekalb PAC $2,500, Groundwork Project PAC $2,500, Democratic Majority Action $1,000); $21,200 in August; September $6,500 (Reflector) or $11,500 incl. Engineers Political Education Committee $5,000 (ADN). December 2025: more than 7,000 donors, more than 6,000 contributions under $100.

history.office: U.S. Senate (Doug Jones for Senate Committee C00640623; candidate S0AL00156)

superpac_donors.pac: Highway 31 (2017 special election; spent 'more than $4 million' opposing Roy Moore)
donors: Senate Majority PAC ('predominantly funded by SMP')

money_history.office: U.S. Senate (Doug Jones for Senate Committee C00640623; candidate S0AL00156)

corp.t: Business and trade-group PAC money in his Senate career, e.g., American Institute of CPAs $10,000, Charter Communications $7,500, National Apartment Association $6,000, and Comcast/NBCUniversal and Lockton $5,000 each (2020 cycle). Other-committee receipts totaled $875,252 (2017–18) and $1,943,850 (2019–20), a mix of business, labor, party and ideological PACs. In 2017 the Highway 31 super PAC, 'predominantly funded' by Senate Majority PAC, spent more than $4 million against his opponent; SMP's own donors were not retrieved. No corporate contributions were reported in his 2026 state filings. His reported PAC money there is mostly labor, party and Democratic-politician PACs.

lobby.t: FEC-itemized pro-Israel PAC contributions in the 2019–20 cycle: NORPAC $5,150, JACPAC $5,000, Friends of Israel PAC $5,000, DMFI PAC $3,000, Pro-Israel America PAC $1,000 ($19,150 total). Track AIPAC has no entry for him, and 2017–18 pro-Israel PAC itemization could not be retrieved.

note.t: Not a current federal officeholder, so no current Senate disclosure. LegiStorm's index shows Senate disclosure filings 2017–2021 (candidate, annual and termination reports), each year with extension letters; contents were not reviewed. No Alabama Ethics Commission statement of economic interests was found. He had not released his tax returns as of Aug. 10, 2026. His stock-trading record as senator was not reviewed.

law_note.t: Jones's own farewell account: 'more than 25 bipartisan bills' passed and signed into law, including repeal of the military widow's tax and permanent HBCU funding. Sponsor-vs-cosponsor counts not verified (congress.gov/GovTrack blocked).

revolving.role: Government relations and white-collar practice (former senator)
revolving.t: Joined in May 2021 with former staffer Cissy Jackson and worked from the D.C. office. One ArentFox LDA registration checked (2022, Infectious Diseases Society of America) does not list him. A full LDA search for his name was not run.

democracy.t: After losing his own race, publicly congratulated President-elect Joe Biden ('my friend of over 40 years') and Vice President-elect Kamala Harris.

debates.note: Says his campaign accepted invitations from several organizations (number not stated) and challenged Tuberville to a series of five debates; no debate has been scheduled because Tuberville declined.

townhalls.period: July–Oct 2026 (documented: Dothan July 22, Huntsville ~July 29, Daphne Oct. 2; part of a 'statewide Town Hall Tour')

note.t: Born (1954) and raised in Fairfield, Alabama; educated at Alabama schools; career in Birmingham. He and his wife have claimed a homestead on their Mountain Brook home since 2010. After 2021 he worked from a Washington law office, which he says was remote work that did not change his residence.

checks.legal: CourtListener was blocked by this environment's proxy, so federal dockets were not searched directly. Searched news archives (AP, APR, Alabama Reflector, ADN, Lagniappe, Wikipedia) for criminal or civil cases, Senate Ethics complaints and bar discipline involving Jones. None found. Alacourt is paywalled and was not searched.
checks.foreign: FARA: the bulk FARA files (all registrants, short-form registrants, foreign principals) were searched by exact name on 2026-10-13 by the records collector and re-checked here; the loose name matches in that output are other people, and nothing matches this candidate. No foreign-government or foreign-business ties appeared in news coverage; his 2017–2021 Senate disclosures were not opened.
checks.claims: Fixed sample: campaign Priorities page read directly (first 10 items are mostly promises; 2 checkable figures rated). The 'Meet Doug' bio page has no reachable URL, so bio claims came from his written statement to Lagniappe. Ads: his two most-covered 2026 TV ads (Sept. 9 data-center ad; Oct. 2 data-center/gas-prices ad) plus his Sept. 2 stock-trading claims. Ad spending is unknown. UPDATE 2026-10-08: Priorities page re-read; its items 1–3 and 5–8 are promises with no checkable figures. Added 2 checkable claims from the first TV ad (Sept. 9, 2026): tax breaks (true) and 'pushing to build' (partly). The second ad's (Oct. 2) script is behind ADN's paywall, so its specific claims could not be read.
checks.democracy: Not in the Senate for the Jan. 6, 2021 count (term ended Jan. 3, 2021). Searched news for his statements on the 2020 and 2024 results; found his Nov. 2020 congratulations to Biden. No statement on 2024 results found. Re-checked 2026-10-08: Wikipedia and The Atlantic (July 2026) contain no statement by Jones disputing 2020 or about 2024 results or Jan. 6. He was not a member of Congress at the Jan. 2017 or Jan. 2021 counts, so certification votes do not apply.

ak-sen-dan-sullivan.name: Dan Sullivan

profile_line.t: Two-term Republican senator, first elected in 2014 over Democrat Mark Begich and re-elected in 2020; endorsed by Donald Trump and Sen. Lisa Murkowski; second in the Aug 18 top-four primary with 41.4%.

oneliner.t: Two-term Republican U.S. senator (since January 2015), former Alaska attorney general and natural resources commissioner, and retired Marine Corps Reserve colonel; he finished second in the Aug. 18, 2026 top-four primary (41.4%) behind Democrat Mary Peltola.

born.note: Wikipedia gives the date; the election pamphlet confirms the birthplace and age 61.

upbringing.t: Raised in Fairview Park, a Cleveland suburb, the son of Sandra and Thomas C. Sullivan. His father was president and CEO of RPM International, the coatings and chemicals company founded by his grandfather Frank C. Sullivan; his brother Frank C. Sullivan became RPM's CEO in 2002. He graduated from Culver Military Academy in Indiana in 1983, then Harvard (B.A. economics, 1987) and Georgetown (joint J.D./M.S. Foreign Service, 1993). He married Julie Fate, daughter of Fairbanks figures Hugh 'Bud' and Mary Jane Fate, in 1994; they have three daughters.

profile.office_years_note: U.S. Senate Jan 2015–present (~11.75 yrs) + Alaska Attorney General 2009–2010 + Alaska DNR Commissioner 2010–2013 + Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary of State 2006–2009 (appointed). White House/NSC staff and Marine service not counted.

career.role: Marine Corps infantry officer (active 1993–97, 2004–06, early 2009, Afghanistan July 2013; Reserve from 1997; retired as colonel 2024)
career.org: U.S. Marine Corps / Marine Corps Reserve

career.role: Law clerk to Judge Andrew Kleinfeld
career.org: U.S. Court of Appeals, Ninth Circuit (Fairbanks)

career.role: Law clerk to Chief Justice Warren Matthews
White House Fellow; director, International Economics, NSC/NEC staff
Assistant Secretary of State for Economic, Energy and Business Affairs
Alaska Attorney General (appointed by Gov. Palin)
Commissioner of Natural Resources (appointed by Gov. Parnell)

platform.t: Says he has expanded oil and gas production in NPR-A, ANWR and Cook Inlet and advanced the Alaska LNG project to lower costs and create jobs.

Says he passed laws to strengthen salmon runs, reduce bycatch and ban imports of Russian and Chinese trawl-caught fish; in 2026 proposed a Bycatch Reduction Act requiring salmon excluders and tougher seafloor-contact accountability for trawlers.

Campaigns on what he calls the largest military and Coast Guard buildup in Alaska's history, including a $7 billion JBER recapitalization, four icebreakers homeported in Alaska and reopening the Adak Navy base.
Credits himself with tax cuts for families, small businesses and seniors and a $1.4 billion federal investment in Alaska's health system.
Strong supporter of Israel and an Iran hawk; lead cosponsor in 2025 of the U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act and the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act.
Opposes abortion except in cases of rape, incest or a threat to the mother's life.

promises.t: Keep expanding Alaska oil and gas production and push the Alaska LNG project forward.
Pass his Bycatch Reduction Act (mandatory salmon excluders, seafloor-contact accountability, federal money for gear testing and electronic monitoring).
Continue the Alaska military and Coast Guard buildup (icebreakers, Adak, JBER).

claims.claim: Sworn in as Alaska's eighth U.S. senator on January 6, 2015, and re-elected in November 2020.

record.t: Senator since January 2015; beat Mark Begich in 2014 and Al Gross 54%–41% in 2020.

claims.claim: Serves on Armed Services, Commerce, Environment and Public Works, and Veterans' Affairs.

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same four committees, including chairmanship of the Armed Services readiness subcommittee.

claims.claim: UVA's Center for Effective Lawmaking ranks him among the Senate's top 10 most effective members.

record.t: The Center ranked him 8th among Senate Republicans in the 115th Congress and, per his own release, the most effective Republican senator on environment policy in the 116th. Neither source shows a top-10 rank among all senators.

claims.claim: Served over 30 years as a Marine Corps infantry officer and retired in early 2024 as a Reserve colonel.

record.t: Commissioned 1993, mostly in the Reserve after 1997 with active stints in 2004–06, 2009 and Afghanistan in 2013; retired in 2024 as a Reserve colonel.

claims.claim: Deployed to the Middle East, Afghanistan, and the Taiwan Strait and South China Sea.

record.t: A six-week Afghanistan deployment in July 2013 is documented, and the election pamphlet lists War on Terrorism Expeditionary and Afghanistan Campaign medals. No source reviewed documents the Taiwan Strait/South China Sea deployment.

claims.claim: Was Assistant Secretary of State, Alaska Attorney General and DNR Commissioner.

record.t: Assistant Secretary of State 2006–2009 (unanimously confirmed), Attorney General 2009–2010, DNR Commissioner 2010–2013.

claims.claim: Was a National Security Council director under Condoleezza Rice.

record.t: White House Fellow and NSC/NEC director 2002–2004. Rice was National Security Advisor then, not Secretary of State (she took that post in Jan. 2005), so the page’s title for her is inaccurate.

claims.claim: His Save Our Seas Act and Save Our Seas 2.0 Act were signed into law by President Trump.

record.t: He introduced SOS 2.0 in June 2019 and Trump signed it on Dec. 18, 2020; the original act was signed in October 2018 (sponsor not shown in the source). 'Most comprehensive in history' is characterization.

claims.claim: Harvard B.A. in economics; joint law degree and foreign-service master's from Georgetown.

record.t: B.A. 1987 Harvard; J.D./M.S.F.S. 1993 Georgetown.

claims.claim: Married to Julie Fate Sullivan for over 30 years, with three daughters.

record.t: Married in 1994; three daughters.

claims.claim: Was massively outspent by national Democrats in both of his Senate races.

record.t: Total 2014 and 2020 outside spending on each side was not obtained (OpenSecrets is blocked to this tool; FEC IE tables did not load).

claims.claim: A Marine Corps Reserve colonel with 25 years of service and the only senator still serving in the military.

said.where: campaign Issues page, intro (claim #1 of sample)

record.t: Outdated text still on the live site: he retired from the Reserve in 2024, as his own 'Meet Dan' page says, so he is no longer serving.

claims.claim: Passed historic ocean cleanup legislation.

said.where: campaign Issues page, item 8 of first section

record.t: Save Our Seas 2.0, which he sponsored, became law in December 2020.

claims.claim: Confirmed 218 federal judges, including two Supreme Court justices.

said.where: campaign Issues page, item 5 of first section

record.t: Judicial confirmation totals were not checked against Senate records. The count reflects a 2020-era page that has not been updated.

claims.claim: Mary Peltola voted against a pay raise for Alaska's troops.

said.where: Sullivan campaign TV ad (most-covered ad #1, per FactCheck.org)

record.t: She voted against the House's July 2023 NDAA over Republican amendments, then voted for the final compromise bill that kept the 5.2% raise. Sullivan voted for the same final bill.

claims.claim: Peltola had 'zero bills signed into law in two terms.'

said.where: remarks launching his campaign's anti-Peltola website (most-covered statement #2)

record.t: Congress.gov/GovTrack enactment counts for Peltola could not be reached. FactCheck.org notes one Peltola-cosponsored NDAA amendment became law, but that is not a bill she sponsored.

claims.claim: The Petersburg Dan J. Sullivan is a sham candidate working with Peltola and Democrats to confuse voters and 'rig' the election.

said.where: statements and NRSC letter (Alaska's News Source)

record.t: The only documented links are Dan J. Sullivan's use of Amber Lee, a consultant who has worked for Democrats, and small 2022/2024 ActBlue gifts to Peltola from 'a Dan Sullivan from Petersburg.' The elections director cited no evidence of coordination, a Superior Court judge ruled the Division of Elections’ new "good faith" test had no basis in law (he did not rule on coordination), and Peltola's campaign and the challenger deny it.

said.t: Hawkish pro-Israel, anti-Iran stance; lead cosponsor of the 2025 U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act.

did.t: Supported the 2024 supplemental aid package for Israel, Ukraine and other allies; earlier cosponsored the Israel Anti-Boycott Act (2017).

said.t: Election pamphlet says he passed legislation to reduce bycatch.

did.t: His Bycatch Reduction Act is described in August 2026 as a proposal, a reworked 2022 research task-force bill; no enacted bycatch law was identified in sources reviewed. Peltola and an Alaska Beacon commentary say he is among the trawl sector's top campaign-money recipients (no figures given).

said.t: Campaigns on support for troops and the Alaska military buildup.

did.t: Voted for the final FY2024 NDAA conference bill with the 5.2% pay raise.

promises_prev.promise: Repeal the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare).

evidence.t: He opposed the ACA and voted to repeal it; the law was not repealed. His campaign site now says he 'repeals negative aspects of Obamacare' (e.g., the Cadillac tax).

complicating.t: In December 2025 he was one of four Republicans voting to advance a Democratic bill extending enhanced ACA premium credits (per the AK key-vote pass); the dates of individual repeal votes were not pulled here.

promises_prev.promise: Build a road to the Ambler mining district (secure the right-of-way).

evidence.t: In June 2024 he added a rider to the FY2025 NDAA requiring BLM to grant the Ambler right-of-way; it was dropped from the final bill.

complicating.t: Later executive-branch actions on Ambler were not researched here.

entries.t: Withdrew support for Trump after the Access Hollywood tape.
Said he would vote for Trump; voted to acquit in both impeachment trials.
Endorsed second-term policies including DOGE spending cuts in his address to the Legislature; Trump endorsed his re-election (July 2025).
Has said 'the verdict is still out' on the human contribution to climate change.
Came out against Pebble after recordings suggested executives planned a larger mine.

aipac_endorse.t: Not confirmed — Track AIPAC does not label him AIPAC-endorsed; AIPAC's own endorsement page was not checked (as of 2026-10-08).

aipac_pac.note: 2026 cycle, Q1 2026 only: Alaska Public Media reports AIPAC passed about $250,000 in earmarked individual contributions to his campaign in the first quarter. Later quarters not obtained.

udp.note: Track AIPAC shows $0 in pro-Israel independent expenditures (data 7/5/26).

others.name: Track AIPAC career 'Israel Lobby Total' (donations from AIPAC, COPAC, NATPAC, RJC, NORPAC and their large donors)

israel.votes_note: Roll-call votes are handled by the key-vote pass (ak-senate-votes.json), not here.

statements.t: Lead cosponsor of the U.S.-Israel Defense Partnership Act and the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act of 2025; has repeatedly urged direct retaliation against Iran over Houthi attacks and has visited Israel/the region at least three times since Oct. 7, 2023.
Cosponsored the Israel Anti-Boycott Act (S. 720).

fec.committee: C00570994 (Alaskans for Dan Sullivan); leadership PAC True North PAC (C00571000)
fec.instate_note: Q1 2026 only: in-state donors were about 17% of his total (Alaska Public Media).
fec.src_note: Six-year election totals Jan 1, 2021–Jul 29, 2026. pac_all = FEC 'other committee contributions' (business, trade, ideological and leadership PACs combined; split not available). 'other' = $3,212,070.34 transfers from authorized committees (joint fundraising) + $311,524.48 other receipts + $9,375.85 offsets. The ~$250,000 AIPAC earmark in Q1 2026 sits inside itemized individual money. In Q1 2026 PACs gave about $277,000 (~24% of his quarter), mostly industry, trade, legal, lobbying and contractor PACs (Alaska Public Media).
fec.quarters_note: Q1 2026 reported as $1.7M (Alaska Public Media) or $2.1M (Straight Arrow News citing Politico); the two figures conflict and neither was checked against the filing.

support: Senate Leadership Fund — announced plans to spend $15M (planned, not confirmed as spent)
Last Frontier PAC (pro-Sullivan super PAC; anti-Peltola ads; amount not found)
oppose: Right For Alaska (super PAC, Hudson, Wis.) — ~$574,000 opposing him, Jul 30–Aug 7, 2026 (OpenSecrets). Its total spending in the race, including promoting Southworth and Heikes, was $2.2M by Aug 18 (NYT via Election Law Blog); FEC shows $2,353,093 in independent expenditures through Sep 30.
907 Initiative — more than $1M on negative ads and information campaigns featuring him (Alaska Public Media)

fec.outside_note: No FEC independent-expenditure totals for the race loaded (tables are script-rendered). Amounts above are from news reports at the dates given. Across the whole race, Alaska Public Media (Oct. 2, 2026) reports independent groups have spent more than $31 million since the Aug. 18 primary, about 70% on opposition; groups backing Sullivan have outspent groups backing Peltola by nearly $7 million.

history.note: Six-year totals 2015–2020.

corp.t: PAC money is a large share of his fundraising: $2,604,358 in other-committee contributions in the 2021–26 cycle, $2,462,069 in 2015–20 and $834,683 in 2014. Alaska Public Media found his Q1 2026 PAC money (~$277,000, about 24% of the quarter) came mostly from industry, trade, legal, lobbying and contractor PACs. A Peltola-campaign post and an Alaska Beacon commentary call him a top recipient of trawl-industry money, but neither gives a figure.

lobby.t: Pro-Israel money: Track AIPAC lists $789,874 in career donations from pro-Israel PACs (AIPAC, COPAC, NATPAC, RJC, NORPAC) and their large donors. AIPAC passed about $250,000 in earmarked contributions to him in Q1 2026 alone.

money2.note: Funders of Senate Leadership Fund and Last Frontier PAC (pro-Sullivan) were not obtained. Opposing groups: Right For Alaska's FEC summary (thru Sep 30, 2026) shows $2,375,017 raised — $1,285,000 from party committees and $990,000 from other committees (names not shown on the summary page) plus $100,000 from individuals (William Harris of Lexington, Mass., per OpenSecrets). 907 Initiative's funders were not found.

networth.note: No assets-minus-liabilities range was computed. The Alaska Current puts his reported assets at $4.1M–$12.3M; Quiver Quantitative (via Newsweek) estimates net worth near $8.4M. Largest asset: RPM International stock listed at $1M–$5M, plus a rental property up to $500,000.

trades.period: STOCK Act filings to Jan 2024 (Disclosed Capitol count; full range not shown)

note.t: The Alaska Current says he has sold about $800,000 of RPM stock in office, is the most active stock trader in the Alaska delegation, and reported some trades late (2018 and 2022). It reports trade timing; it does not document that he acted on non-public information. Peltola's campaign says he 'tripled his wealth'; the Alaska Current's review says trades roughly tripled his wealth. Senate eFD was not searched directly. He sold shares of RPM International, the coatings company his family has long been tied to, in Sept. 2018, Feb. 2020 (after a CDC briefing, about two weeks before pandemic shutdowns) and Nov. 2022 (a month before weak earnings). Reporting documents the timing, not any use of nonpublic information, and no committee of his directly oversees the company, so these sales are not counted as committee-overlap trades.

committees: Armed Services (chairs Readiness and Management Support subcommittee)
effectiveness.note: Sponsored/enacted counts not retrieved (congress.gov not reached). Enacted examples: Save Our Seas 2.0 (2020).

democracy.t: Voted against the objection to Arizona's electoral votes (objection failed 6–93).
Voted against the objection to Pennsylvania's electoral votes (failed 7–92).
Voted against creating an independent commission to investigate the Jan. 6 Capitol attack.

After the Electoral College vote, acknowledged Joe Biden as president-elect, saying his oath is to the Constitution and the laws of the nation, though the result was not what he and many Alaska Trump voters hoped for.

access.note: He took part in a fisheries debate in Kodiak with Peltola (described on Peltola's campaign site). He did not answer the Alaska Beacon voter-guide questionnaire. Totals for debates accepted/declined and town halls were not found.

note.t: Ohio native. Election pamphlet lists 29 years in Alaska: Fairbanks 1997–98, Anchorage 1998–2002 and 2009–present. In 2014, a tax assessor said he was a Maryland resident during his State Department years, when he claimed Bethesda as his primary residence but voted absentee in Alaska.

checks.legal: CourtListener, Justia, Senate eFD, House/Senate Ethics, APOC and Alaska CourtView were all unreachable from this environment (proxy 403 / fetch provenance block), so no court or ethics database was searched directly. News searches (this pass: Senate Ethics complaint; earlier pass: lawsuits/charges) found no lawsuit, charge or Senate Ethics complaint against Sen. Dan S. Sullivan; the 2026 complaints found concern the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg. Only compliance item remains the late STOCK Act reports (2018, 2022).
checks.foreign: Senate eFD unreachable; news coverage of his disclosures mentions no foreign assets. Exact-name check of the DOJ FARA bulk files (registrants, short forms, foreign principals), searched 2026-10-13: no row names this candidate (the only near match is a 'Daniel J. Sullivan III' of SST Aerospace, Greenville SC, 2019 — a different person).
checks.claims: Mechanical sample: (a) every checkable claim on the campaign 'Meet Dan' page (dansullivanforalaska.com/meet-dan/): 11 rated (items on independent-voter share and his winning coalition are not checkable/opinion); (b) the first 10 items on the Issues page (first section 'Getting It Done in Washington'): intro claim (25 years/only serving senator) rated misleading, #8 ocean cleanup rated true, #5 judges unverifiable; #1 COVID, #2 ANWR/NPR-A, #3 '25% Obama cuts', #4 $300M water/sewer, #6 2A, #7 Green New Deal, #9 $50M public safety, #10 Alaska Native are opinion or were not checked. The Issues page appears to be largely 2020-era text. (c) Ad spend unknown; most-covered items: the campaign's 'pay raise' ad (FactCheck.org) and his Sept. 3, 2026 'zero bills' remarks. Also rated: his sham-candidate accusation against Dan J. Sullivan.
checks.democracy: Certification votes from senate.gov roll calls (records profile: Nay on the Arizona and Pennsylvania objections, 2021). Statements: ADN Dec. 14, 2020 (acknowledged Biden as president-elect); Alaska Public Media Jan. 4, 2021 reported he had not said in advance how he would vote. No 2024-result statement searched beyond this.

legal.t: Filed periodic transaction reports late for two RPM stock trades from March and May 2018 (filed late July 2018); he said his managers did not tell him in time. The Alaska Current says he was also cited in 2022 for STOCK Act reporting violations, with the same explanation.
legal.status: Reported late; no penalty or ethics finding documented in sources reviewed

recordx.note: 'late' refers to STOCK Act transaction reports in 2018 and 2022, not annual reports (annual-report timeliness not checked). Missed-vote % not obtained (GovTrack not reached). FEC RFAI/notices tab did not load. The key-vote pass records him Not Voting on roll 119-2-252 (Sept. 29, 2026).
recordx.added: Missed-vote rate: 28 of 915 roll calls in the 119th Congress, from the official roll-call record (Oct 18, 2026). FEC filing record: 19 requests for additional information (RFAI) to their committees, from FEC filings (Oct 17, 2026).

gaps: Senate eFD annual reports and PTRs (net worth range, full trade list) not read directly
Funders of Senate Leadership Fund, Last Frontier PAC (pro-Sullivan) and of 907 Initiative and Right For Alaska's party/committee donors (anti-Sullivan)
Business vs. ideological split of PAC money; trawl-industry totals
Checks on Issues-page numbers ($300M water/sewer, 218 judges, '25% cuts') and election-pamphlet figures ($7B JBER, four icebreakers, Adak, $1.4B health)

wiki.t: Daniel Scott Sullivan (born November 13, 1964) is an American politician, attorney, and Marine Corps veteran serving as the junior United States senator from Alaska, a seat he has held since 2015. A member of the Republican Party, he served from 2010 to 2013 as commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources and from 2009 to 2010 as Alaska Attorney General.

ak-sen-mary-peltola.name: Mary Peltola

profile_line.t: Democrat and former at-large U.S. representative who lost the House seat to Nick Begich in 2024; she entered the Senate race on Jan 12, 2026 and led the primary with 49.5%.

oneliner.t: Yup'ik Democrat and former U.S. representative (Sept 2022–Jan 2025), the first Alaska Native in Congress, who lost the House seat to Nick Begich in 2024 and led the Aug. 18, 2026 Senate primary with 49.5%.

born.note: Date from Wikipedia; Anchorage birthplace also in her Alaska Beacon questionnaire. Her election pamphlet says only 'Alaska'.

hometown.t: Bethel, Alaska (raised along the Kuskokwim River)

upbringing.t: Daughter of Ward Sattler, a Nebraska-born pilot and teacher, and Elizabeth 'LizAnn' Williams, a Yup'ik woman from Kwethluk. She grew up in Kwethluk, Tuntutuliak, Platinum and Bethel, began fishing with her father at six and registered as a fishing captain at 14. She studied elementary education at the University of Northern Colorado (1991–93) and took courses at three University of Alaska campuses (1994–98) without a degree listed. Her husband Eugene 'Buzzy' Peltola Jr. died in a September 2023 plane crash; she has four children and three stepchildren.

profile.office_years_note: Alaska House 1999–2009 (10) + Bethel City Council 2011–2013 (2) + U.S. House Sep 2022–Jan 2025 (~2.3). Tribal court judge 2020–21 not counted.

education.deg: Coursework in elementary education, no degree listed
education.school: University of Northern Colorado; UAF, UAS, UAA

platform.t: Running on lowering gas, grocery, health care, housing and childcare costs; says she would cut taxes and raise wages.

Proposes 12-year congressional term limits, a ban on members and immediate families owning or trading individual stocks, the DISCLOSE Act ($10,000 disclosure threshold), and a constitutional amendment overturning Citizens United.
Would ban factory trawling, keep mid-water trawlers off the sea floor, seek fishery-disaster money and add Tribal seats to the North Pacific Fishery Management Council.
Says she supports oil and gas development; her September 2026 energy plan backs Alaska LNG and more in-state refining.
Opposes Medicaid cuts; would restore Medicaid money and reinstate ACA premium tax credits.
Says abortion decisions belong to a woman and her doctor; backs gun rights (NRA member per her pamphlet; NRA endorsed her in 2024).
Opposes the war with Iran and says she would have backed war-powers measures to halt it.

promises.t: Push 12-year congressional term limits and a congressional stock-ownership ban.
Ban factory trawling and reduce bycatch to restore salmon runs.
Reverse health-care cuts and fund the Alaska Marine Highway, the Railbelt grid, public radio and education.

claims.claim: Served in the Alaska House 1999–2009, on the Bethel City Council 2011–2013 and in the U.S. House 2022–2025.

said.where: 2026 election pamphlet bio (substitute — campaign 'My Story' page unreachable)

record.t: Same dates in Wikipedia and Ballotpedia (U.S. House Sept 13, 2022–Jan 3, 2025).

claims.claim: Lived in Bethel, Kwethluk, Tuntutuliak and Platinum before moving to Anchorage in 2025.

record.t: Wikipedia lists the same four Kuskokwim communities.

claims.claim: Attended the University of Northern Colorado, UAF, UAS and UAA.

record.t: UNC 1991–93 and University of Alaska campuses 1994–98; no degree listed (she does not claim one).

claims.claim: Executive Director, Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission.

record.t: Wikipedia lists her as executive director after 2016; Ballotpedia says interim executive director. Whether she holds the job now was not confirmed.

claims.claim: Two of her sons have served in the U.S. Coast Guard.

record.t: No independent source reviewed.

claims.claim: NRA member.

record.t: Membership is not independently documented; the NRA did endorse her in 2024.

claims.claim: 'Pushed through the largest pay increase for our soldiers in decades.'

said.where: Peltola TV ad (most-covered ad #1, per FactCheck.org)

record.t: The 5.2% raise in the FY2024 NDAA was the largest in more than 20 years and she voted for the final bill, but the raise followed the statutory Employment Cost Index formula; FactCheck.org calls 'pushed through' subjective. Her one enacted NDAA amendment was unrelated to pay.

claims.claim: Introduced legislation to open ANWR and NPR-A to oil development.

said.where: campaign energy rollout (Sept 2026), as reported by Fox News (most-covered #2)

record.t: She co-led Alaska's Right to Produce Act with Rep. Pete Stauber in 2023, then urged Democrats to vote against the floor version over a provision nullifying the Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area, and later filed a version without it.

claims.claim: She secured the reversal that let ConocoPhillips' Willow project move forward.

said.where: campaign energy rollout, per Fox News

record.t: She publicly backed Willow with both Alaska senators; sources reviewed do not show her role as decisive.

claims.claim: Sullivan remains the 'top recipient' of Big Trawl campaign cash.

record.t: The post relies on an opinion column and op-ed that give no figures; OpenSecrets industry data could not be reached.

claims.claim: Sullivan 'tripled his wealth in office' and made up to $2 million as a stock trader.

record.t: An Alaska Current review of disclosures says his trades roughly tripled his wealth, but its $2 million figure describes estimated trade volume, not profit. Disclosure ranges make exact gains unknowable.

claims.claim: She owns no stocks.

record.t: Her 2025 House disclosure, as summarized by Newsweek, lists retirement and 529 accounts and 'some investments' but no itemized holdings were reviewed; the Alaska Current says she reported no trades in office.

said.t: 'I support oil and gas development'; touts bills to open ANWR and NPR-A.

did.t: Co-led Alaska's Right to Produce Act and voted for it in committee, then urged House Democrats to oppose the floor version over a Bering Sea provision; she later introduced a version without it.

said.t: House record broke with most Democrats in support of Israel.

did.t: Voted for the February 2024 stand-alone Israel aid bill (one of 46 Democrats) and in May 2024 for the bill to stop the administration from withholding arms to Israel (one of 16 Democrats). In 2026 her campaign would not say whether her views have changed.

said.t: Ad says she pushed through the largest troop raise in decades.

did.t: Voted for the final FY2024 NDAA containing the 5.2% raise (after voting against the House version in July 2023).

saydo.note: Same vote as the pay-raise claim in the claims check; scored once there.

promises_prev.promise: Restore salmon runs by curbing trawl bycatch (2022–24 House campaigns).

evidence.t: Introduced the Bottom Trawl Clarity Act and Bycatch Reduction and Mitigation Act in May 2024; neither became law before she left office.

complicating.t: 53 trawl interests and fishery stakeholders urged her to withdraw the bills, calling them unworkable. House Republicans controlled the floor in 2023–24.

entries.t: Co-chaired the Blue Dog Coalition (May 2023–Jan 2025) and voted with Republicans on several immigration-enforcement bills.

wiki.t: Mary Sattler Peltola (born August 31, 1973) is an American politician and former tribal judge who served as the U.S. representative for Alaska's at-large congressional district from 2022 to 2025. ballot.t: Filed May 29, 2026 as a Republican three days before the deadline, registered to vote as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom opened an investigation, citing 'credible allegations' of coordination; the NRSC demanded his removal. Elections Director Carol Beecher disqualified him (determination dated June 15) for not filing a 'good-faith' candidacy, citing his name use, his party switch at filing, a website resembling the senator's and his Democratic-linked consultant; she did not cite coordination evidence. Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews reversed on June 26, finding the standard had no legal basis, and the Alaska Supreme Court affirmed on June 29 and left the ballot listing to the division. He appears with no party label. After finishing third, he declined to withdraw by Aug 31, citing in part the removal of his Republican label.

Supports neighborhood, charter and correspondence options, but says public money should go only to public schools. Protect Medicaid expansion; expand telehealth; cut red tape on housing construction and child-care businesses; lower electric bills through utility cooperation and renewables.

Calls fiscal instability his top issue. Backs corporate income tax 'parity' for oil and gas, including privately held S-corporations, and North Slope development. Says he would put forward a balanced budget.
Would have signed HB 78, which restores a defined-benefit pension for public employees. Supports the 2024 voter-approved minimum-wage and paid-sick-leave law, while open to changes.

Pitches bipartisan governance and calls himself the 'opposite' of Gov. Dunleavy, whom he describes as combative and partisan.

Districts have closed or planned to close schools: Fairbanks closed seven in five years, and Anchorage plans to close three. record.t: KTUU (July 2025) linked DPS 'Crime in Alaska 2023' and the Criminal Justice Data Analysis Commission's 2024 report as support for the declining-crime claim. wiki.t: Tregarrick R. "Treg" Taylor (born May 19, 1976) is an American lawyer who was the Alaska attorney general from 2021 to 2025. He succeeded Ed Sniffen, who resigned after being appointed to the position two weeks before. Taylor is a candidate in the 2026 Alaska gubernatorial election. He was disqualified due to failure to comply with financial disclosure requirements, but this was later reversed.

oneliner.t: First-term Republican congressman from Chugiak, a software-company founder and investor, who has held Alaska's at-large seat since January 2025; Trump-endorsed, he led the Aug. 18, 2026 top-four primary with 44.6% and faces independent Bill Hill, Democrat Eric Hafner and Libertarian Jim McDermott in the Nov. 3 ranked-choice general.

He earned a BBA from Baylor University and an MBA from Indiana University, worked for Ford Motor Company (2002–2004, per his own pamphlet), and has lived in Alaska since 2004 (Anchorage to 2011, Chugiak since). His grandfather, Rep. wiki.t: Jerry Lee Carl Jr. (born June 17, 1958) is an American politician and businessman who served as the U.S. representative for Alabama's 1st congressional district from 2021 to 2025. A member of the Republican Party, he previously served as a member of the Mobile County Commission from 2012 to 2020, the last two years as president of the commission. His district is based entirely in southern Alabama, encompassing parts of Mobile along with all of the state's portion of the Gulf Coast.

profile_line.t: Republican representing east Alabama since 2003 and chairman of the House Armed Services Committee.

oneliner.t: Republican from Calhoun County who has represented east Alabama's 3rd District since 2003 and chairs the House Armed Services Committee; a former county commissioner and state House minority leader, he won the May 19, 2026 GOP primary and faces Democrat Lee McInnis.

hometown.t: Blue Mountain / Saks area, Calhoun County, Alabama (family left Calhoun County in 1957 for work and returned in 1967)

upbringing.t: Rogers was born in Hammond, Indiana, after his family left Calhoun County to find work; they returned in 1967. His father, Clyde Rogers, was a firefighter at Anniston Army Depot, and his mother, Linda Perryman Rogers, worked at a textile mill (Classe Ribbon Company); his official bio says he grew up in the Blue Mountain mill village. He graduated from Saks High School, earned a political science degree (1981) and an MPA (1984) at Jacksonville State University, and a law degree with honors from Birmingham School of Law (1991), the same year as his wife, Beth. He then opened a law practice in Anniston. He married Beth Phillips, now a Calhoun County district judge, in 1982; they have three children.

upbringing.t: Aderholt is the only child of Mary Frances Brown and Bobby Ray Aderholt, who served as an Alabama circuit judge for about 30 years and was a part-time minister. He graduated from Haleyville High School in 1979, attended the University of North Alabama, and earned a B.A. in history and political science from Birmingham-Southern College (1987) and a J.D. from Samford's Cumberland School of Law (1990). He practiced law, was appointed Haleyville municipal judge in 1992, and became a legal aide to Gov. Fob James in 1995 before winning the open 4th District seat in 1996. He married Caroline McDonald, daughter of former state senator and Agriculture Commissioner Albert McDonald, in 1994; they have two children.

wiki.t: Robert Brown Aderholt ( AD-ər-hohlt; born July 22, 1965) is an American politician and attorney from Alabama. A socially conservative member of the Republican Party and a member of the Tea Party Caucus, he is currently serving as a U.S. representative, representing Alabama's 4th congressional district since 1997. The district includes most of Tuscaloosa County north of the Black Warrior River, as well as Birmingham's far northern suburbs in Walker County and the southern suburbs of Huntsville and Decatur.

al-07-terri-sewell.name: Terri Sewell

profile_line.t: Birmingham Democrat who has represented the 7th District since 2011 and is Alabama's only Democrat in Congress besides Figures.

oneliner.t: Birmingham Democrat and former public-finance lawyer who has represented Alabama's 7th District since January 2011 and sits on the Ways and Means Committee.

born.t: January 1, 1965, Huntsville, Alabama (Wikipedia only; not confirmed in a second source)

upbringing.t: Raised in Selma. Her father, Andrew A. Sewell, was a high-school basketball coach; her mother, Nancy Gardner Sewell, was a high-school librarian and later a Selma city council member. Wikipedia says she was Selma High School's first Black valedictorian. After Princeton, Oxford (Marshall Scholar) and Harvard Law, she clerked for Chief U.S. District Judge U.W. Clemon in Birmingham, practiced securities law at Davis Polk & Wardwell in New York, and returned to Alabama in 2004 as a public-finance lawyer at Maynard, Cooper & Gale. The family and early-life details rest on Wikipedia alone in this research.

education.deg: M.A. (Marshall Scholar; Wikipedia lists the Oxford degree as a bachelor's in political science)

career.role: Law clerk to Chief Judge U.W. Clemon

platform.t: Lead sponsor of the Voting Rights Advancement Act, later renamed the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act; backs expanded early voting.
Supports Medicaid expansion and incentives for states to adopt it. Backs bills to lower prescription-drug costs, fund rural hospitals and study health disparities.
Supports abortion rights; opposed Alabama's Human Life Protection Act and the 2022 Dobbs decision.
Supports a $15 federal minimum wage.
Her 2014 campaign site listed education, health care, and jobs and the economy as her issues.

claims.claim: Graduated from Princeton (1986), studied at Oxford as a Marshall Scholar (1988) and earned a Harvard law degree (1992).

The Clerk's roll call confirms H.R. 4 passed the House 228–187 on Dec. 6, 2019 (she voted Aye). The House later agreed to H.Con.Res. 107 renaming it for John Lewis. The sponsor line itself could not be opened on congress.gov (blocked to the fetch tool); verdict changed from unverifiable to true on this basis.

She bought Apple and Nvidia shares in April 2025 and sold GE HealthCare and Tapestry shares in March 2026, all reported on PTRs.

did.t: Voted Yea on H.R. 1834, the three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits (passed 230–196).

profile_line.t: Democratic governor, first elected in 2022, renominated without opposition. Her running mate for the new lieutenant governor office is former Mesa Mayor John Giles (2014–2025). Giles was a Republican for decades and changed his registration to independent in May 2026. She declined the Oct 6 Clean Elections debate.

oneliner.t: Democratic governor of Arizona since January 2023, a former social worker, state legislator (2011–2019) and Secretary of State (2019–2023), seeking a second term with independent John Giles as her running mate.

hometown.t: Tempe, Arizona (grew up there; Seton Catholic High School, 1988)

upbringing.t: Kathleen Marie Hobbs was born in Phoenix and grew up in Tempe in a middle-class family with a twin sister, Becky; at times the family relied on food stamps and, in her own account, on its church community. She graduated from Seton Catholic High School (1988), earned a bachelor's in social work at Northern Arizona University (1992) and a master's in social work at Arizona State University (1995), and worked as a social worker, including as chief compliance officer at the Sojourner Center domestic-violence shelter. She married Patrick Goodman in 1996; they have two children. She is Catholic.

career.role: Social worker; chief compliance officer, Sojourner Center (domestic-violence shelter); adjunct professor at Paradise Valley Community College and ASU

platform.t: Campaigns on bringing down prices; touts middle-class tax cuts, a senior deduction, no state tax on tips and overtime, repeal of the tax on rent, and down-payment help for first-time buyers.

Cites ending state-land leases of Saudi-owned Fondomonte, which farms with Arizona groundwater and ships crops overseas.
Cites sending the National Guard to the border and funding local law enforcement for border security and anti-trafficking work.
Says she will keep working to fix the education system; as governor proposed rolling back the universal ESA expansion (2023) and later an ESA accountability plan (2024).

promises.t: Keep bringing down costs for families, fix the state's education system and keep Arizona safe (stated reelection focus).

did.t: Ordered the Arizona National Guard to the border (Dec 17, 2023) and now campaigns on the deployment and on funding local law enforcement for border work. She vetoed SB 1164 (2025), which would have required state and local cooperation with federal immigration detainers.

promises_prev.promise: Repeal Arizona's pre-Roe near-total abortion ban, through the Legislature first or a 2024 ballot measure

evidence.t: Signed the repeal of the 1864 ban on May 2, 2024; it took effect Sept 14, 2024. Voters then passed Proposition 139 (2024), protecting abortion up to fetal viability.

complicating.t: The repeal needed votes from a few Republican legislators in a GOP-controlled Legislature. The constitutional protection came from a citizen initiative, not from her.

promises_prev.promise: Roll back the 2022 universal expansion of the Empowerment Scholarship Account (voucher) program

evidence.t: Her 2023 executive budget and first State of the State called for rolling back the expansion, which she said could cost $1.5B over a decade. In January 2024 she shifted to an eight-point accountability plan (background checks, manual approval of purchases over $500) instead of repeal. Superintendent Tom Horne said she had shifted her view.

profile_line.t: U.S. representative for AZ-05 (not seeking re-election to the House), Trump-endorsed. He won the July 21 Republican primary with about 73% over Rep. David Schweikert. His running mate for lieutenant governor is Sine Kerr, a Buckeye dairy farmer and former state senator (2018–2025) whom the Trump administration named Arizona state executive director of the USDA Farm Service Agency in 2025.

upbringing.t: Andrew Steven Biggs was born in Tucson. As a young man he served a Latter-day Saints mission to Japan and became fluent in Japanese. He earned a B.A. in Asian studies at Brigham Young University (1982), married Cindy Biggs that year, and earned a law degree at the University of Arizona (1984). He practiced at a firm in Hobbs, New Mexico, then became a prosecutor in Phoenix. In 1993 he won $10 million in the American Family Publishers sweepstakes. The couple have six children; a daughter, Cosette, died of cancer in 2025.

Fight for Arizona's Colorado River allocation; long-term water strategy via WIFA; measure aquifers; desalination, recycling and Bartlett Dam storage; repeal Hobbs's executive order prioritizing wind and solar on state land; promote mining.
End state incentives and subsidies; require data centers not to draw power or water away from homes and businesses; leave zoning to localities.
Protect Empowerment Scholarship Accounts; opt into the federal education tax credit; emphasize core academics and trade pathways.

'Make Arizona Healthy Again' agenda: end medical mandates, over-the-counter ivermectin, raw-milk sales, SNAP junk-food limits. Says there is significant Medicaid fraud, especially among able-bodied single adults.
Sign election bills Hobbs vetoed; speed up results; ensure only eligible citizens vote.

wiki.t: Andrew Steven Biggs (born November 7, 1958) is an American politician and lawyer serving as the U.S. representative for Arizona's 5th congressional district since 2017. A member of the Republican Party, Biggs served as a member of the Arizona House of Representatives from 2003 to 2011 and a member of the Arizona Senate from 2011 to 2017. legal.t: The Clean Elections Commission (unanimously, Aug 27, 2026) directed its director to finish investigating whether her campaign actually collected its $5 qualifying contributions. About 74% of 5,000 donor names were shared with two other campaigns; six listed donors told the Arizona Mirror they never gave. The campaign deposited the $5 total in one lump sum on May 4, the day it applied. Collins also alleges two unreported subcontractors. The Attorney General is also investigating (Mirror, Sept 11). Her attorney, Tim La Sota, denies fraud but acknowledged she violated Clean Elections rules by signing forms for contributions she did not personally collect, saying she was confused. Possible outcome: an order to repay up to $2.8M, from personal funds if campaign cash is short.
legal.status: Investigations pending; no commission finding or repayment order and no criminal charge as of Oct 14, 2026. Her suit was dismissed Sept 30 as premature, and the Court of Appeals then declined to take the case. On Oct 8 the Arizona Supreme Court agreed to hear it (conference set for Oct 14; no ruling found). The candidates refused to comply with commission subpoenas; on Oct 6 the commission denied their motion to quash and extended its civil investigation past the Oct 29 deadline. Her attorney says the letters forced the campaigns to suspend.

recordx.note: No federal or legislative record. State filing compliance is the subject of the pending Clean Elections case, recorded under legal.

She beat Hugh Lytle, the chair-backed candidate, by about 1,200 votes while raising about $40,000 to his $2.1 million. Her running mate for lieutenant governor is Angela Harrolle Mohan, a registered independent and former CEO of The 100 Club, a nonprofit for families of fallen public-safety personnel.

az-01-amish-shah.name: Amish Shah

links.site_note: Home and About pages read directly. The Issues page (amishforarizona.com/issues) could not be opened from this environment.

profile_line.t: Emergency physician and former state representative (2019–Feb 2024) who lost this seat to Schweikert 52%–48% in 2024. He won the four-way 2026 Democratic primary with 39.4%.

oneliner.t: Emergency physician and former Arizona state representative (2019–Feb 2024) from Phoenix; the 2024 Democratic nominee, he lost AZ-01 to David Schweikert 51.9%–48.1%, then won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary over DCCC-backed Marlene Galán-Woods by about 3,700 votes. He faces Republican Jay Feely and Libertarian Monica Alponte.

born.t: 1977 or 1978 (exact date not documented), Chicago, Illinois
born.note: Both sources give Chicago. Wikipedia's infobox gives only an age range (48–49).

upbringing.t: Raised in Chicago. His Gujarati parents immigrated from India in the 1960s while pursuing engineering degrees; his father is Jain and his mother Hindu. He earned a B.A. in economics (1997) and an M.D. (2001) at Northwestern, then an M.P.H. at UC Berkeley (2003). After an emergency-medicine residency in New York City and faculty work at Mount Sinai, he moved to Arizona for a sports-medicine fellowship at the University of Arizona and later practiced at Mayo Clinic Arizona. He entered politics after a Scottsdale meeting encouraged him to run, and campaigned door to door at the urging of then-House minority leader Eric Meyer.

career.role: Emergency-medicine resident (New York City), then faculty and researcher

career.yrs: 2008–2009 seasons (AP, per his campaign); Wikipedia says five seasons

career.role: Emergency physician (salary $227,913.93 in 2025; $84,825 in 2026 to mid-July)
State representative, LD24 (2019–2023) and LD5 (2023–Feb 2024); ranking member, Health & Human Services in his final term
Contract emergency physician (The Emergency Center; US Acute Care Solutions); president, AMS Emergency Services LLC; board member, Arizona College of Emergency Physicians

platform.t: Health care: his 2024 site backed universal health care; he campaigns on lowering health-care and prescription-drug costs. KJZZ reports he has never said he supports a government-run (socialized) system.

Abortion: his 2024 site called him '100% pro-choice' and said he personally gathered more than 1,200 signatures for the abortion-access ballot initiative. His 2026 home page lists abortion rights among the things he would defend.
Housing/education: supports wider pre-K access and federal incentives for affordable housing in Arizona; his 2024 site called for higher teacher pay and school funding.
Border: supports securing the U.S.–Mexico border.
Democracy: his 2024 site pledged to oppose gerrymandering and the influence of money in politics.
Israel: backs a two-state solution and Iron Dome/defensive weapons for Israel; criticized Israel's current prime minister (June 2026 forum). Details in the israel block.

promises.t: Accept no contributions from corporate PACs.
Defend Social Security, Medicare, abortion rights and the rule of law.
Work across party lines.

profile_line.t: Former NFL placekicker (1999–2014, including the Arizona Cardinals 2010–2013). He launched his campaign in AZ-05 in April 2025 and switched to AZ-01 in December 2025. Endorsed by Donald Trump, he won the GOP primary with 49.8%.

oneliner.t: Former NFL placekicker (14 seasons, 2001–2014, including the Arizona Cardinals 2010–2013) turned CBS analyst, from Gilbert. A first-time candidate, he launched in AZ-05 in April 2025, moved to AZ-01 in December 2025, and with Trump's endorsement won the July 21, 2026 Republican primary over state Rep. Joseph Chaplik. He faces Democrat Amish Shah and Libertarian Monica Alponte.

hometown.t: Tampa area, Florida (Jesuit High School, Tampa)

upbringing.t: Grew up in the Tampa area. His father, T.J. Feely, a former College of St. Thomas running back, owns the Feely Kicking School of Tampa, and his grandfather coached basketball and baseball at St. Thomas. At Tampa's Jesuit High School he set Hillsborough County kicking records, and at 16 he played on a national-champion youth soccer team. He kicked for Michigan from 1994 to 1998, including the 1997 national-title team. Undrafted in 1999, he played arena football before reaching the NFL with Atlanta in 2001. He and his wife, Rebecca, have four children and live in Gilbert.

wiki.t: Mohamed Zuhdi Jasser (born November 17, 1967) is an American religious and political commentator and a medical doctor specializing in internal medicine and nuclear cardiology in Phoenix, Arizona. Jasser is a former Lieutenant Commander in the United States Navy, where he served as staff internist in the Office of the Attending Physician of the United States Congress. In 2003, with a group of American Muslims, Jasser founded the American Islamic Forum for Democracy (AIFD) based in Phoenix, Arizona, and in 2004 he was one of the founders of the Center for Islamic Pluralism.

upbringing.t: Born in Hilo, Hawaii, he spent much of his childhood there and also lived in Arizona, the Philippines, Panama and Argentina, graduating from Chandler High School in 1990. He moved to Utah and started a paintball business (Paintball Junkeez) that went bankrupt in 2003, then returned to Arizona and worked in pest control. He spent about six years with the Salt River Pima–Maricopa Indian Community police before joining the Pinal County Sheriff's Office in 2012, and was elected sheriff in 2016. He and his wife Janel have been married since 1994 and had five children; a son, the son's fiancée and their infant daughter were killed in a 2022 Gilbert traffic crash, which he cited when he entered the race. He is a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.

After retiring she earned a bachelor's (American Military University, 2013) and master's (Grand Canyon University, 2019), worked in veterans outreach and nonprofits, and was a veteran services representative for Rep. Tom O'Halleran. She ran for the Arizona Senate in 2020 and lost. She is a single mother of a son.

profile_line.t: Republican incumbent since January 2023, re-elected in 2024 with 50.0%; unopposed in the 2026 primary.

oneliner.t: Two-term Republican congressman from Tucson (since January 2023), a Mexican-born naturalized citizen and former senior adviser to Gov. Doug Ducey, on House Appropriations, seeking a third term against Democrat JoAnna Mendoza in toss-up AZ-06.

born.note: Birthplace in both; date from Wikipedia only.

upbringing.t: Born in Hermosillo, he came to Tucson as a young boy with his parents and two younger sisters through a port of entry; the family became lawful permanent residents with help from their church. His father drove a bus. He attended Tucson public schools (Rincon High School), Pima Community College and the University of Arizona, working maintenance and fast-food jobs, and was the first in his family to graduate from college. He worked for the University of Arizona and the Tucson Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, then as a senior adviser to Gov. Doug Ducey and vice chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission (2015–2021). He and his wife Laura have six children.

profile.office_note: U.S. House since Jan. 3, 2023. His Arizona-Mexico Commission vice chair role (2015–2021) was an appointed post on a governor's commission and is listed under career, not counted here.

platform.t: Defends H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) for no tax on tips and overtime, an expanded/permanent child tax credit and small-business investment incentives; opposes higher taxes.

Says the law's work and reporting requirements target 'waste, fraud, and abuse' and protect the programs; says he fought steeper Medicaid cuts in earlier drafts and backed the $50B rural hospital fund.
Defended starting the 2026 war so Iran cannot get nuclear weapons; opposed ground troops and opposed war-powers limits; said in May 2026 the war was 'very close to being over.'
Supports border security legislation; reportedly open to protections for people brought here as children; supported White House handing the Minnesota enforcement operation to Tom Homan.
Praised Dobbs; opposes a nationwide ban; supports Arizona's 15-week law; criticized the 2024 ruling reviving the 1864 ban.
Co-signed a May 2025 letter warning against Trump administration plans to downsize the Social Security Administration.

wiki.t: Juan Ciscomani III ( SIS-koh-MAH-nee; born August 31, 1982) is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for Arizona's 6th congressional district since 2023. A Republican, he was a senior adviser to former Governor Doug Ducey and vice chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission. Ciscomani was chosen to deliver the Republican response to the 2023 State of the Union Address in Spanish.

profile_line.t: Democrat who won the 2025 special election to succeed her late father, Raúl Grijalva, and was sworn in Nov 12, 2025. She was unopposed in the 2026 primary.

oneliner.t: Democratic congresswoman from Tucson, a former Pima County supervisor and longtime TUSD board member, who won the Sept. 23, 2025 special election to succeed her late father and was sworn in Nov. 12, 2025 after a seven-week delay; unopposed in the 2026 primary, she faces Republican Daniel Butierez for the third time on Nov. 3.

hometown.t: Tucson, Arizona (south side; Pueblo High School)

upbringing.t: A lifelong Tucsonan who grew up with two sisters on the city's south side and graduated from Pueblo High School (1989, per Wikipedia). Her grandfather came from Mexico as a bracero in 1945; her father, Raúl Grijalva, represented the area in Congress until his death in March 2025 — his record is his own. She earned a political science degree at the University of Arizona, directed the Pima County Teen Court diversion program for about 25 years, and was elected to the TUSD board in 2002. She is married to Sol Gómez, a librarian, and they have three children.

career.org: Pima County Teen Court (juvenile diversion; Pima Prevention Partnership benefit plan since 1996)

career.role: U.S. Representative, AZ-7 (Natural Resources; Education and the Workforce)

platform.t: Supports abolishing ICE, saying it cannot be reformed; no objection to border security or port-of-entry modernization; supports a permanent path to citizenship for DACA recipients.

Opposes the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship rules (says they burden people whose names changed through marriage); defends mail voting; does not trust federal control of elections and raised the prospect of ICE agents at polling places.
Supports single-payer Medicare for All; cosponsored the Medicare For All Act and a bill restoring ACA premium tax credits.
Accused the Israeli government of genocide in Gaza in a 2025 debate; cosponsored the Block the Bombs Act to halt certain military aid to Israel.

Criticized the Bureau of Reclamation for exempting Upper Basin states from Colorado River cuts; wants data centers to use waterless cooling; opposes the Oak Flat copper mine, citing San Carlos Apache concerns.

Fight 'Trump's economic chaos'; defend Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and the VA; affordable housing; environmental justice; fully fund public education; humane immigration; tribal sovereignty; 'people-centered' foreign policy.

profile_line.t: Republican in Congress since 2011 (first elected in 2010), re-elected here in 2024 with 65.3%; unopposed in the 2026 primary.

oneliner.t: Republican dentist from Flagstaff who has served in the U.S. House since January 2011 (AZ-1, then AZ-4, now AZ-9). The House censured him in November 2021. Trump-endorsed, he was unopposed in the July 21, 2026 primary and faces Democrat Danielle Sterbinsky on Nov. 3.

upbringing.t: Born in Rock Springs and raised in Pinedale, Wyoming, the eldest of ten children (seven sons, three daughters) of Republican parents; his grandparents were Slovenian and Basque immigrants. He earned a B.S. (1981) and a D.D.S. (1985) at Creighton University in Omaha, then ran a dental practice in Flagstaff from 1989 until his 2010 election, served as Arizona Dental Association president (2004–05), and had never held elected office before 2010. His brother Pete Gosar is a former Wyoming Democratic Party chair, and six siblings appeared in 2018 ads backing his Democratic opponent; their actions are theirs, not his.

Voted in 2023 for H.Con.Res. 21 directing removal of U.S. troops from Syria; in Oct. 2022 invited Zelenskyy and Putin to Arizona for peace talks.

A member of the Democratic Party, he served as the 28th mayor of Long Beach, California, from 2014 to 2022. He was both the city's youngest and first elected openly LGBT mayor, as well as the first Latino to hold the office. He is the second person of color to be mayor of Long Beach, after Republican Eunice Sato, a Japanese American who served from 1980 to 1982. A former member of the Long Beach City Council, he was vice mayor from 2012 to 2014.
wiki.title: Robert Garcia (California congressman)

wiki.t: Trayvon Benjamin Martin (February 5, 1995 – February 26, 2012) was an African American from Miami Gardens, Florida, who was fatally shot in Sanford, Florida, by George Zimmerman, a 28-year-old Hispanic-American. Martin had accompanied his father to visit his father's fiancée at her townhouse at The Retreat at Twin Lakes in Sanford. On the evening of February 26, 2012, Martin was walking back to the fiancée's house from a nearby convenience store. Zimmerman, a member of the community watch, saw Martin and reported him to the Sanford Police as suspicious. Several minutes later, an altercation occurred and Zimmerman fatally shot Martin in the chest.

wiki.t: Matthew Dunlap (born November 26, 1964) is an American politician from Maine who has served as the Maine state auditor since November 2022. He previously held the same position from January to October 2021. A member of the Democratic Party, Dunlap was secretary of state of Maine from January 7, 2013, to January 4, 2021, and previously from 2005 to 2011. In 2012, he sought to become his party's nominee to replace retiring Olympia Snowe, but lost in the primary to State Senator Cynthia Dill. He is currently the Democratic nominee for Maine's 2nd congressional district in the 2026 election, facing off against Paul LePage.

wiki.t: Alice Glass Kirkpatrick (October 11, 1911 – December 9, 1976), best known as Alice Marsh, was an American socialite and political hostess who was the long-time mistress of U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson. Their affair began in 1938 and ended in the 1960s due to Marsh's disagreement with Johnson's policy regarding the Vietnam War. Throughout this period, they were both married to other people (Johnson to Lady Bird Johnson and Marsh, starting in 1940, to several successive men) but they continued to have an ongoing intimate relation, although their sexual relation may have ceased.

ny-06-grace-meng.name: Grace Meng

wiki.t: Grace Meng (Chinese: 孟昭文; pinyin: Mèng Zhāowén; born October 1, 1975) is an American lawyer and politician serving as the U.S. representative for New York's 6th congressional district since 2013. Her district is situated within the New York City borough of Queens; it includes Bayside, East Elmhurst, Elmhurst, Flushing, Forest Hills, Fresh Meadows, Glendale, Jackson Heights, Kew Gardens, Maspeth, Middle Village, Woodside and Rego Park. A member of the Democratic Party, Meng represented the 22nd district in the New York State Assembly from 2009 until 2012. She is the first Asian American to be elected to the United States Congress from New York.
